speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I rise to take part in this debate for the purpose of correcting various misstatements that have been made by a few hon. members in discussing radio broadcasting, and to answer unfounded statements that are being currently circulated inside and outside this house.
All hon. gentlemen are well aware that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is an autonomous body created by act of parliament. The corporation has full authority to plan and carry out policies within the scope of its act and within the funds which by the act are placed at its disposal. The Minister of Transport is designated by the act as the means of communication from the corporation to the government and to parliament. I think it is unfortunate in many ways that a member of the board of governors of the corporation cannot himself be the spokesman in parliament, but as this is impracticable, I assume it to be my duty to correct misstatements as they occur in this house.
It is a happy reflection on parliament that the subject of radio broadcasting has never been used for purposes of party advantage. There have been three committees of parliament on this subject, and the findings of all three were unanimous. Two bills affecting radio broadcasting have passed the house, in both cases unanimously. In the debate which instituted broadcasting as a public service, hon. members in all parts of the house took part, and all favoured the bill.
Perhaps I can summarize the purposes which promoted the founding of public control of broadcasting by reading short extracts from two or three of the speeches made on that occasion. The first is from the speech of the then prime minister, which summarized admirably the reasons why legislation for public ownership was adopted:
No other scheme than that of public ownership can ensure to the people of this country, without regard to class or place, equal enjoyment of the benefits and pleasures of radio broadcasting. Private ownership must necessarily discriminate between densely and sparsely populated areas. This is not a correctable fault in private ownership; it is an inescapable and inherent demerit of that system. It does not seem right that in Canada the towns should be preferred to the countryside or prosperous communities to those less fortunate. In fact if no other course were possible, it might be fair to suggest that it should be the other way about. Happily, however, under this system, there is no need for discrimination; all may be served alike. Equality of service is assured by the plan which calls for a chain of high power stations throughout Canada.

The Address-Mr. Howe
The opposition spokesman was the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), who said:
I just wish to endorse the views expressed by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, to say that I am in full accord with the principle embodied in this bill. I have been supporting this principle from the first, more particularly after the work of the Ail'd commission, but I knew the difficulties in the way and the strength of the propaganda carried on to prevent the woi'k of that commission from having the results which we have witnessed to-day.
I am pleased with the work which was done by the committee which has been studying this question, and I congratulate the members of that committee on the excellent work which they did. I congratulate the house upon having this bill introduced at the present session, and I congratulate the people of Canada on the principle which is represented in the bill.
The third party was spoken for by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) who said:
I should just like to associate myself with the last speaker (Mr. Lapointe) in congratulating the Prime Minister on his promptness in bringing down this bill to implement the report which has been unanimously adopted.
Perhaps I may take two or three moments to give a brief outline of the development of public broadcasting in Canada. At the time the Aird commission was appointed to study the matter, about fifty per cent of the broadcasting strength of Canada was represented by four privately owned stations, two in Toronto and two in Montreal. Each of these stations was attached to a United States broadcasting chain, and the programs broadcast over them were almost entirely of United States origin. Apart from these cities very few communities were served by radio. The Aird commission, composed of Sir John Aird as chairman, and Mr. Augustin Frigon and Mr. C. A. Bowman, made a thorough investigation of the whole situation. The commission took evidence in Canada and in the United States and travelled in Europe, and after much study brought down a comprehensive report. The recommendations of the commission were, briefly, that the control and operation of radio broadcasting in Canada be made a public utility, and that the government should estab-ish its own high power broadcasting stations so that complete coverage of Canada would be obtained by this means.
The report was brought in too late for the then government to implement it, and it was not until 1932 that a parliamentary committee was set up to review the subject again. That parliamentary committee brought down a report which was the basis of the broadcasting act of 1932. In 1934 a second parliamentary committee studied the question and again brought in a report, suggesting revisions of
the commission plan of management and a return to the basis recommended in the Aird report. However, no change was made at that time. In 1936 a third parliamentary committee studied the subject and brought in a unanimous report which was made the basis of the present broadcasting act. The act now in force was studied by that committee and recommended by it to this house after it had unanimously approved the draft bill.
The revenues of the corporation were provided, at first, by a licence fee of one dollar, which was in force for the period prior to the establishment of public broadcasting, and the proceeds of which were used for a very important service that is apt to be forgotten now-the elimination of interference with broadcasting. A considerable expenditure, some $300,000 I believe, is made each year on this service, and I can tell the house that without the abolition of interference with broadcasting there would be very little reception in any part of Canada to-day, even in the large cities. It is a most important work, and if the service were relaxed for two or three years broadcasting would rapidly become impossible.
The Aird report recommended that revenue to carry out the public ownership program should be provided, first from a licence fee of $3 per radio set, second, from advertising revenue to the amount of $700,000, together with a grant from the dominion government of $1,000,000 per annum. It was estimated, I believe, that the funds from these three sources would amount to about $3,500,000 per annum. As I stated, a radio fee of one dollar was put into effect in the initial period. When broadcasting was set up as a public service the fee was raised to two dollars and at that figure it has remained.
During the current fiscal year about 1,150,000 persons will pay licences of two dollars, and the sum realized, less the cost of collecting these licences, that will accrue to the broadcasting corporation from this source, will approximate closely $2,000,000. The corporation will earn this year about $350,000 from all commercial sources, and that is the highest level of commercial revenue that the corporation has received to date. It is not the desire or intention of the corporation at any time to obtain a revenue of over $500,000 from commercial sources for reasons that are obvious.
The mandate given to the broadcasting corporation set up by the last broadcasting act was detailed in the report of the committee on radio for 1936. It recommended (a) "that a public corporation, modelled more closely on the lines of a private corporation,
The Address-Mr. Howe

but with adequate powers to control, for purposes of coordination, all broadcasting, both public and private, be set up to replace the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission;" (b) "that this corporation be known as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to be managed by a general manager as chief executive, and an assistant general manager, and directed as to policy by a non-partisan board of nine directors or governors, chosen in order to give representation to all parts of Canada;" and (c) "that the corporation immediately consider ways and means of extending national coverage."
It is that last mandate to which I wish to call attention. One of the first acts of the newly constituted broadcasting corporation was to make a coverage survey of Canada. That coverage survey disclosed that less than fifty per cent of the population of Canada had adequate coverage from existing sources. The corporation had certain funds at its disposal under the broadcasting act; it had also the privilege of borrowing from the dominion government the sum of $500,000 as a repayable loan. With that amount and with some $200,000 saved from current revenues, the corporation set about carrying out its mandate to establish high-power broadcasting stations. Two of these stations have been built, each of 50 kilowatt capacity, one near Montreal and one near Toronto. These stations were undertaken first because, through them, efficient coverage could be provided for a maximum number of listeners.
The corporation wishes to continue to carry out its mandate and establish adequate coverage by building two more stations and improving certain other properties where equipment is obsolete. With that in mind its governors have recommended to the government that the radio fee be now increased from $2 to $2.50, and that fees be collected for each radio set rather than from each owner of one or more radio sets. The main purpose, as I say, is to provide revenue sufficient to justify the expense of establishing two high-powered stations in sparsely settled areas of this dominion. In addition to the fifty cent increase in licence fee, another repayable loan of $500,000 will be required. In reviewing the work of the corporation and the results accomplished to date it seems to me that the request of the corporation is a reasonable one.
Also let me say that there is an urgency for the completion of coverage which it is well to draw to the attention of the house. In 1932 the distribution of wave lengths between the countries of North America was considered by an international conference. A division was made by which Canada received

the use of six exclusive wave lengths; the United States received certain others, as did also other countries. In addition to these exclusive wave lengths Canada secured the partial use of other wave lengths, suitable for low-powered stations. Within a year or two broadcasters desiring to establish high-powered stations and not able to obtain wave lengths in the United States discovered that Mexico was not a party to this international agreement, and that the Canadian channels were not being used by high-powered stations, so these men simply moved over to Mexico and established high-power stations there using exclusive Canadian channels. The result has been that not one of the six channels allotted to us is free from interference from Mexican sources. The interference from Mexican sources conflicts seriously with the coverage of the Canadian stations using those channels.
As a result of this interference Canada has protested vigorously to the other countries which are parties to the convention. Preliminary conversations were held with our near neighbours at a conference at Havana some months ago, and about six or seven weeks ago a full conference of all American countries was held at Havana. At that time a new allocation of wave lengths was made. Instead of six clear channels Canada secured seven, and also secured a more favourable distribution of partly used channels. But this stipulation was made, and I think for a good reason, that unless Canada would proceed to establish on each of these exclusive wave lengths a radio station of at least 50,000 watts power the other countries would not guarantee that that wave length would remain exclusive to Canada. It was pointed out to our delegates at that conference that Canada was at fault if its exclusive wave lengths had been interfered with, because Canada had not made anything like adequate use of them. Therefore the matter is urgent because the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is under compulsion to complete the establishment of its high-powered stations on the newly acquired wave lengths. The corporation has laid down the policy that if funds can be made available the high-powered stations necessary for complete coverage will be built within the next year. It has shown to me conclusively that the funds from the sources I have mentioned will be adequate to complete the work, and no one can see any reason! to anticipate that funds from any source other than those mentioned will at any time be required to enable the corporation to carry out its functions in the years to come.
I wish at this time to discuss a matter which has been the subject of much mis-

The Address-Mr. Howe
representation both in the house and outside, the use of American programs. I shall tell you how the ninety-eight hours of operation per week of the network are divided. Let me say that a sustaining program means a program devoid of advertising-having no advertising of any kind, direct or indirect; a commercial program means a program which contains advertising in varying amounts. Of the ninety-eight hours broadcasting on the network, fifty-seven and one quarter hours are given up to Canadian programs free from advertising, three and one-quarter hours are occupied by commercial programs originating in Canada, and seventeen and one-half hours are devoted to American programs free from advertising. Programs originating in the British Isles, and free from advertising, account for twelve hours, a German program occupies half an hour, and advertising programs originating in the United States occupy eight and three-quarter hours. The total percentage occupied by non-advertising programs is 87-8. The present American commercial programs have for some years been distributed in Montreal, Toronto and Windsor.

speechtext: Would the minister be good enough to identify the week of which he is giving an analysis?

It is any week within the last five. I am speaking now of the chain.
There has been a good deal of misrepresentation about the distribution over station CBL, so perhaps I might give the distribution there. CBL is an individual station operated by the corporation, forming part of the chain of the corporation, but of course it operates for longer hours than the chain. The network operates twelve hours a day, and this station I suppose is on the air some eighteen or twenty hours a day, therefore it has more advertising programs than the chain. However, the total commercials on GBL (Toronto) represent thirty-five per cent of the total time of that station. American commercials represent eighteen per cent of the time, and Canadian commercials seventeen per cent.
In one of our great financial journals there was published a chart showing the American programs, and at the bottom of this chart there appeared the words "The flood of American advertising coming into Canada." It stated that forty-three per cent of the programs on CBL are American advertising programs.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Where is station CBL situated?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
At Toronto. The fact is that American commercial programs make up
eighteen per cent of the. time and American sustaining programs twenty-five per cent of the time of that station.
Now let me say something about these American programs. As you know, a sustaining program is one put on purely for entertainment purposes. It carries no advertising and mentions no sponsor, but is simply put on for the benefit of the listeners; and, as I say, some fifty-seven per cent of the programs over the Canadian chain are of this type, made in Canada. But may I say that each of the three commercial chains in the United States produce sustaining programs for their listeners. For example the National Broadcasting Company pays the Metropolitan Opera Company a very substantial sum for the privilege of broadcasting the Saturday afternoon performances of that company, The Columbia Broadcasting System pays the New York Philharmonic orchestra a very substantial sum in order to broadcast the performance of that orchestra for two hours on Sunday afternoons. Similarly the Mutual chain supplies certain sustaining programs to please its listeners.
The competition for quality in these sustaining programs is strenuous. A recent development has been that the National Broadcasting Company has retained the services of the great conductor Arturo Toscanini to form an orchestra of his own, to be composed of the best musicians obtainable in New York and that vicinity, to broadcast a series of ten concerts exclusively for the radio. I was told by the president of the National Broadcasting Company that his company is paying Toscanini and his artists 8450,000 for organizing this orchestra and presenting these ten programs exclusively for radio broadcasting.
This type of programs makes up the seventeen hours of sustaining programs that we obtain from the United States. The Metropolitan Opera broadcast takes about three hours a week. The broadcast of the New York Philharmonic on Sunday afternoon takes about two hours. The Toscanini program on Saturday evening takes about one and one-half hours, and any musician will tell you that in the matter of perfection of technique the Toscanini program is the finest musical feature that can be heard anywhere on this continent and perhaps anywhere in the world.
These American sustaining programs are for the most part musical programs. Since when was music anything but international? When we listen to the Metropolitan Opera what artists do we hear? Are they American? Yes, a few of them are, but we hear also Italian, German, French and perhaps Brazilian
The Address-Mr. Howe

artists as well; we hear artists from every corner of the world. Is the music they play
American music? No, it is probably German, Italian, French or Spanish music, with an occasional American composition. So I ask if bringing in the music of the Metropolitan Opera can be called flooding Canada with American propaganda. What nonsense I
We listen to the music of the New York Philharmonic. Who is the conductor of that orchestra? The regular conductor is John Barbirolli, who came to America from Leeds, England. Only a few Mondays ago as guest conductor of the Philadelphia Symphony I heard our own Sir Ernest MacMillan, and at other times we hear distinguished guest conductors from every part of the world. I ask if there is anything offensive to Canadian listeners in accepting that kind of program from the United States? I could go on and give other examples, but I do not think I need labour the point. However, I do say that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation makes no apologies to the Canadian people for bringing them these seventeen hours of American sustaining programs.
One other point I think should be cleared up now. I noticed a question on the order paper asking how much Canada pays the United States for the programs brought into this country. That question of course will be answered in the usual way, but I can say now that Canada pays nothing at all in dollars and cents. No single dollar of ours goes to pay for a program brought in from the United States. But we are not accepting favours from the United States in taking those programs. We have an exchange arrangement with each of the great national chains, which they are just as glad to make as we are, under which those United States chains take our sustaining programs in exchange for their own. I checked up the hours of Canadian programs taken by the great United States chains, and I find they just about equal the hours we take from them. Last night we heard a peroration which concluded with the statement, "the United States speaks; Canada listens." That is true of certain hours. Of certain other hours it is equally true that Canada speaks and the United States listens. I am sorry that the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Marsh) spoiled a very fine maiden speech by ending with such a phony peroration.
Now I come to the commercial programs. As I say, we take eight and three-quarter hours of commercial programs from the United States over our national chain, broadcasting from coast to coast. For broadcasting these programs we receive a gross payment of about

8200,000, of which we pay about 880,000 to the stations that make up our chain as payment for the time used, and we net about
8120,000	to the broadcasting corporation. The programs we take are chosen for their entertainment value, and I may add that we have been offered and have refused additional commercial programs for chain broadcasting which would have netted our corporation an additional amount of over 8250,000. We refused them for the reason that they did not have the class of material that we cared to carry on our Canadian network.
The programs we do broadcast are the most popular programs broadcast in the United States as commercial features. The Charlie McCarthy program, to which reference has been made in this house, is considered the number one program over any American chain. Checks are made of the listeners to individual programs, and it has been shown that the average audience listening to that program whenever it is broadcast exceeds 33.000,000 persons. The cost of building that program, which lasts for one hour each week, is more than the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation can spend on its fifty-seven hours of sustaining programs. In other words more money is spent in building up that one program than we can spend in building up fifty-seven hours of broadcasting. It has been suggested in the house that we should build up a program to put on as a sustaining feature at the time the Charlie McCarthy program goes on. Who would listen to it? We have been doing that for years. The listeners insist on Charlie McCarthy, as has been demonstrated by the listener check-ups that have been made. The material used in the Charlie McCarthy program is, I think, to most people, exceedingly amusing, and therefore we carry that feature on the chain. By doing so we save the cost of building a program which otherwise would have to be provided for that hour.
It has been said that in connection with the cost of carrying programs we are discriminating in favour of United States advertisers. That is absolutely untrue. Rates for chain broadcasting are on the card and apply to any Canadian advertiser who wishes to obtain chain broadcasting privileges, just as they apply to United States sponsors. The rates for chain broadcasting are slightly lower than those applying to the individual stations. However that is only the wholesale rate as against the retail rate. May I say that from the point of view of financial returns we prefer the chain broadcast to the broadcast from an individual station, because the chain

The Address-Mr. Howe
broadcast relieves us of the cost of building a sustaining program for the same period. The rates charged at each station are based on the coverage of that station, and rates in Canada generally, on the basis of coverage, are somewhat higher than those charged by stations in the United States.
For a moment let us look at the broadcasting situation from a common sense point of view. Anyone who has a family knows that, where radio is concerned, there is a wide variation in tastes. One man's radio meat is definitely another man's radio poison. For my own experience I draw on my own family. Occasionally all of us listen to the radio. I like almost any kind of music, provided it is played softly so as not to interrupt whatever else I may be doing. My wife prefers the operatic and symphonic concerts, My two boys, aged fifteen and twelve, go for the sports broadcasts; I refer to the broadcasts of hockey and football games and boxing matches. Those are the sports in which they take part and in listening to the play by play or blow by blow descriptions of the contests they get the same thrill as though they were participating. My two younger girls like the vaudeville. They would have been shocked had they heard the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hyndman) refer to Bill Penner; they would have corrected him instantly, and he would have been told that it was Joe Penner. My older girl of fourteen years has graduated from the class which like vaudeville. She has moved in with her mother, and likes the better class of musical programs. For that I believe I owe a debt to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which makes it possible for us to have the variety of cultural and first class musical programs which come in over Canadian broadcasting stations.

speechtext: It will cost you $2.50, though, for each different taste.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
To work out our family situation I may say that it is necessary to have three radios in our house; otherwise there would be a conflict of interest. However, I will pay those three licence fees cheerfully, and I feel anyone else who wishes to avoid conflict at home might do likewise. I have always regarded the system which charged a two-dollar licence fee on a cheap crystal set, parts for which can be bought for fifty cents, and charged a similar fee for a householder owning four radio sets in his house, and one in his car, as one which discriminated in favour of people of ample means as against those of only limited means. I believe hon. members will agree with me that there would be greater justice in taxing the sets, rather than the houses in which the sets are contained.
The present attacks on the principle of public ownership are being made not because the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a failure but because it is a success. The listening audience in Canada are turning their dials to programs of the corporation. I believe the reason is apparent, and can be readily demonstrated by any hon. member who wishes to try the experiment. If one were to leave his dial turned to a corporation station for the full twelve hour period of broadcast he would find a better average program than he would find if he turned on any other station for a similar continuous period. On that corporation station one finds the programs of ever increasing excellence built in Canada by the corporation. One finds, too, the best programs of the British Broadcasting Corporation, which, broadcast in the evening in England, are received here in the afternoon. We find the best of American sustaining programs, built in the United States, and such few United States commercial programs as have the highest entertainment value.
Naturally when the listening public turns to the publicly owned stations, the privately owned stations fight back. That is what is happening to-day. The fact that the chains are carrying a few of the outstanding advertising programs has caused certain newspapers and periodicals to fear the loss of national advertising revenue. Some of those papers are voicing severe criticism on their editorial pages. It is striking, however, to find that even where severe criticism of the policy is written on the editorial page, the radio page, either full or half size, carries a description of radio programs, and almost invariably those descriptions feature United States commercial broadcasts. So much for consistency in our press.
However, radio in Canada will not be judged by speeches made in parliament, nor will it be judged by the editorials written in our newspapers. It will be judged by the programs that come daily into our homes from the publicly owned stations. Of the verdict, I think, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation need have no fear. In advocating the carrying out of the recommendations of that corporation in the direction of the additional revenues they require to complete the plan of nationalization of radio started in 1928, I have every confidence the people of Canada will approve the recommendations I am making to the government of which I have the honour to be a member.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened very attentively to the speech just delivered by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), and in my opinion it was timely and effective. The most amazing
The Address-Mr. Heaps

thing to me in the whole controversy with respect to the fifty cent increase in radio licences is the fact that when the public are receiving something in return for a fee, and they are asked to pay an increase of twenty-five per cent, there is a great howl from certain quarters, but when, on the other hand, the government levies an indirect tax which takes many dollars each year from the pockets of individuals, we never hear a murmur. This shows the difference in effect between direct and indirect taxation.
I wonder whether those who to-day are criticizing the activities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are entirely disinterested in their criticism. I had no intention of speaking on this question, but I do appreciate the great improvement that has taken place in the programs and service which have been given to the Canadian public since the present corporation took over the management of our radio broadcasting. A few weeks ago I had the opportunity of hearing, over the service provided by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the inaugural speech, known as the message on the state of the nation, delivered by President Roosevelt at the opening of congress. I listened to it most attentively, and had the service not been provided by the corporation I might have missed that splendid opportunity. As I listened to the President of the United States speak to congress on the state of the nation, just prior to the opening of our parliament here, I wondered whether our own government or our own Prime Minister would deliver as definite or as conclusive a speech on the occasion of the opening of our parliament.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that if I do not refer at greater length to the remarks of the minister (Mr. Howe) he will forgive me, because I did not know that I was to follow him in this debate.
When I read the speech from the throne, which was delivered in the other chamber, the thing that struck me most was its barrenness, its nebulous character, its lack of definiteness as to what was in the mind of the government regarding what they were going to do for the people of this dominion.
In the main, Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne contains references to commissions that have been appointed by the government, to the trade agreements which the government have in contemplation, and to the expansion of our foreign trade. In fact our government takes the stand that in the conclusion of trade treaties and the expansion of our trade with foreign nations lies the solution of our problems. I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot agree. Members who 
have been in the house as long as I have will know that at all times I have supported any government that has reduced the tariff. I have always supported the Liberal party in its reduction of tariffs just as I have always opposed the Conservative party in its tariff increases, but I have always taken the stand that moving the tariff up a little or down a little will not provide a solution for our national problems. To-day the bankers of the world are shouting from the roof-tops that the trade of the world should be liberated, that tariffs should be reduced, and I have been wondering since when have the bankers of the world or of this nation become the champions of the ordinary farmer and working man. We should indeed be in strange company if we were found in the ranks of the bankers agreeing with them that a policy of lower tariffs would solve our economic problems. If I thought that that was the solution, Mr. Speaker, I would hold up both my hands immediately for such a reduction and so end all our troubles; but even in low tariff countries to-day, just as in high tariff countries, they have exactly the same problems to face as those by which we are confronted in the Dominion of Canada.

I am glad the Prime Minister takes the position that in international trade is not

The Address-Mr. Heaps
to be found a complete solution of our national problems. We must bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that every nation to-day is anxious to find export markets. In that we are not alone. In fact, since production became simplified and the nations learned to produce with an ease that we did not know fifty or a hundred years ago, practically all nations have had exportable surpluses, and it is because of these exportable surpluses that competition among the nations for foreign markets is becoming keener and keener, while at the same time there is a lessened demand from the nations of the world for the importation of commodities as compared with the demand that existed twenty-five- or fifty or seventy-five years ago.
I maintain that it is not necessary for us to look first of all to foreign markets. The first thing for any government to do is to satisfy the home demand. Can anyone give me a logical reason why we in Canada cannot consume the goods we produce here in such abundance, or why we must not consume them until Japan, China, Germany, Italy and other countries have first been supplied from our production? The people who have first claim on the productive capacity of the dominion are the Canadian people themselves. When we find ourselves with a surplus of commodities, then let us by all means find export markets to take our surplus. But no government has ever yet attempted adequately or even reasonably to satisfy the demands of the Canadian people. Have the demands .of the Canadian people been legitimately met? Certainly not. In this country hundreds of thousands of people, some of them out of work, some of them working part time or full time, are living on the borderline of poverty, and until we have satisfied their legitimate demands their needs should receive first consideration, and foreign countries second. I remember in my school days reading in a history of India the story of the people of India famishing while India was exporting her wheat. We here are doing very much the same thing; we are exporting so-called surplus commodities while hundreds of thousands of Canadian people are in dire want.
The government might claim that as a result of the trade agreements they have made with the nations of the world our trade has increased, but I will not subscribe to that assumption because in all parts of the world trade has increased, and although the tariffs of this country have decreased by only a comparatively small amount during the past two or three years, our imports have jumped up. If tariffs are a hindrance to international trade I would like to ask this question of
economists, who may be able to answer it in a simple way: Why is it that in spite of high tariffs, quotas and other trade restrictions in all parts of the world, there has been this great jump in international trade in the past two or three years? He will begin the cycle in 1929, when we had the peak of trade, and continue down to 1932, and then he will take the upward period from 1932 to 1937. So far as Canada is concerned we find that those years cut right across the political complexions of the governments in office during that time, indicating quite obviously, I think, to almost everyone that the tariff structure of the country had very little significance with respect to the flow of trade so far as Canada is concerned. During that period we were under a Conservative government about the same length of time as we were under a Liberal government. Consequently I say that our tariff structure is not the fundamental factor in trade that we thought it was many years before.
It seems to me that there are features of our trade relations which are akin to the situation of the two families who used to take in each other's washing in order to try to keep themselves busy. This parliament has a grave responsibility. It can sit idly by and, Micaw-ber-like, hope for something to turn up. But I claim it must deal definitely and effectively with the problems that confront us. We must realize the changed world and changed conditions in which we live. Recent years have completely revolutionized the social and economic structure. We cannot deal with present day problems on the basis of ideas that may have served in the nineteenth century. There is no stronger aid to fascism and all that it stands for than to create the impression that parliament is either unable or unwilling to deal effectively with present day economic conditions. I know the great and powerful forces of an economic nature that often stand between a government and needed reforms, but if parliament is all-powerful, as it should be and could be, then such forces as stand in the way of needed economic changes must be swept aside, and the will of parliament and the people must prevail.
In my opinion the masses of this country, in spite of the results of by-elections, still feel that the government of the day is not coming to grips with the real problems that confront us, the paramount one of course being that of economic security. The search for mythical markets abroad may sound alluring to some, but that is not an effective means of remedying conditions at home. There is no reason why in order to distribute amongst our own people the goods produced in Canada we should depend on foreign countries. Must
we tell our people that before we can consume the goods that we produce here we must first find export markets? I think we all realize that our distributive system is out of harmony with the times in which we live. It is not a case of tariff adjustment one way or the other, it is a definite clear case of giving to the Canadian people the fruits of their own enterprise and energy so that they may enjoy the products of their labours.
The time has arrived when hon. members must shed their party labels and think more of their constituents than of the party whips.
I can think of no time when the responsibilities of members of parliament were greater than they are to-day. Throughout the world far-reaching changes are taking place. In all parts we see social and economic upheavals; even in Canada we cannot escape their effects. Under these circumstances it is the bounden duty of parliament so to shape the destiny of this dominion that our people will have grounds for hope that parliament is earnestly dealing with the pressing problems of the day. I am afraid that there is no such impression at present. We are not dealing effectively with the problems of poverty or insecurity. If to-day I ask the house to give some real lead in regard to these social problems it is only something that I have been doing for the past twelve years.
So little encouragement, I regret to say, is afforded in the speech from the throne, that I cannot vote in favour of the address. But it is my earnest hope that the government will yet give the nation a lead, that instead of continuing to be one of the backward nations of the empire in matters of social progress we shall take our rightful place at the head of those countries which are leading the way towards a more just and better social era.

It has been quite a contrast with the debate following the election of 1925, much, I think, to the credit of the present debate. It also has been worthy of note how much of our time during this debate has been spent in discussing fiscal matters, which naturally would be expected to follow the budget. Experience has proved, however, that if you want any changes of a major nature made in the budget you must have them made in advance of the budget speech, because seldom are any but minor
The Address-Mr. Motherwell

changes made after the budget is brought down. Another reason, perhaps, why we have taken so much time in discussing fiscal matters is that we are all concerned with home budgets; hence we are talking about them here in a national way.
The thoughts I have had in mind are expressed to some extent in a statement that has been prepared by the appropriate department showing the fluctuations in our tariffs during the past sixty years. Do not take alarm; I am not going to dwell on each of the sixty years, but I would like to point out the little progress we have made in either direction, up or down-and especially down- during those years. I am going to mention a number of elections which were fought primarily on tariff matters, and when we consider these figures, which I obtained from an accurate source, those of us who believe in low tariffs must ask ourselves if we have been talcing the best possible way to get the greatest results.
In the year of confederation the general tariff on major commodities in which farmers are interested was 15 per cent, and a large number of items are given in the statement I have before me. That situation continued until 1878, when Alexander Mackenzie's administration went out of office. Then and there followed the first battle of tariffs of which I am aware, between the government of Alexander Mackenzie and the party under the leadership of Sir John Macdonald. The former, heading a low tariff party, was defeated; the latter came into power with a high tariff policy which was brought inter force in 1879, when tariffs were shot up pretty generally, almost as they were in 1930.
Later on, in 1891, the Liberals went to the country on a tariff policy of unrestricted reciprocity. Sir John A. Macdonald was still in the saddle. The Liberal policy practically meant a reversion to the old conditions of reciprocity which obtained between 1854 and 1866, but, as might have been expected, our opponents took advantage of the opportunity to alarm the people as to what unrestricted reciprocity would mean, although it had been in force for twelve years. They raised the cry of annexation. So thoroughly was that campaign carried on that I almost voted Tory myself, because I did not at all like the idea of annexation, and if unrestricted reciprocity meant that, then I did not want any of it. We are not so scared by these cries now as we were in those days, although the fact that Edward Blake resigned the leadership of the Liberal party at that time because he thought unrestricted reciprocity would lead in that direction, gave some colour to the cry raised
rMr. Motherwell.]
by our opponents. Seeing that they are so prolific in the production of cries of that nature I am not so much surprised that they took advantage of that opportunity, and, as already stated, almost converted your humble servant to their way of thinking.
That was in 1891, and that was a terrific battle of tariffs. Then in 1894, when Sir George Foster was Minister of Finance, a considerable reduction was made. You will remember that period, I think; he was going to lop off, and did lop off, the mouldering branches of protection. Consequently there was a considerable reduction in that year, especially on farm implements. That did not save the government of that day from defeat. I have found that death-bed repentances on the part of governments, in connection with tariffs or anything else, do not amount to very much. They are not very effective. By the time that active repentance comes along the mind of the people is pretty well made up and you might as well save your last moment repentance, because you are going to get it in the neck anyway.
Following the election of 1896 there was a considerable reduction of tariffs, though the reductions were not so great as they would have been if Sir George Foster had not anticipated it and reduced tariffs himself, although without any beneficial results to his party. In 1897 again there were considerable reductions, though not nearly what we had hoped for. Anyway, we kept on living in hope, until finally in 1911 the great proposal for freer trade with the American republic was brought down in the form of what is known as the reciprocity agreement.
On that occasion again our friends of the Conservative party excelled themselves in propaganda as to the horrors that this would lead to, in the matter of annexation. I do not want to picture this too vividly; that seems to be their major cry in any campaign and especially with respect to tariffs and treating our neighbours more generously. The election of 1911 resulted in the defeat of the Liberal party. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that inasmuch as the Liberal party, with Sir Wilfrid Laurier at its head, sacrificed its political life on behalf of Canadian, and particularly western, agriculture, it always seemed to me most ungrateful that a third party should spring up at a later date, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was still available for endorsation. Let me repeat that. The Liberal party went out of power in 1911 fighting on behalf of Canadian agriculture, particularly in the west.

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
Then in 1917 there was another general election. The less we say about that election the better. It was not on tariffs; it was on a lot of other things, the War-time Elections Act and such like. Then in the latter part of 1921 the first King administration came into power, and our policy was to reduce tariffs by "easy stages" of about two and a *half per cent at a time. I think it was my hon. friend the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) who coined that phrase when he wanted to allay the fears of the protectionists, when he was at the head of the Progressive party. I am afraid my own leader adopted it later on. Those easy stages, I think, are sound economically, but they are absolutely no good politically. You nip off a little bit here, a little bit there and a little bit somewhere else, but the aggregate is not nearly so apparent as when you take it and cut it in two. So I would in a friendly way warn the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) not to be too easy in his stages of tariff reductions. However in 1930, when the Dunning budget was brought down, in justice to my own party and my own leader I was proud-and am still proud-to say that we had the lowest tariff since confederation on implements of production. But the issues of high or low tariff do not seem to figure very much in a campaign in which the tide is either for or against you. For instance, the low tariff province of Saskatchewan split nearly even in 1930. Only eleven Liberals were elected out of twenty-one and the rest were either Conservatives or members of some other adverse group.
Then, in September of the same year, after the Liberals had been condemned for low tariffs by a province which should have known better, the people voted for a party which shot up the tariff, not by easy stages, but like a sky-rocket. All that happened despite the fact that tariff was not the predominant issue of the election of 1930. We will remember that butter figured far more conspicuously than the tariff did. Nevertheless the right hon. the leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Bennett) on that occasion lived up to his promises and, in a twinkling, gave us higher tariffs throughout Canada. I do not know whether that was the right way to do it, but it did not work out very well for his party.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It worked well for the country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The people soon changed their minds. Hard times steadily grew harder, and by 1935 we did not hear any more talk about high tariffs; the leader of the 51952-17
Conservative party then wanted reciprocity with the United States. That was a remarkable conversion, in some respects almost greater than that of St. Paul. I do not think there was ever a more zealous campaign against any issue than that which was lodged by the present leader of the opposition throughout Canada against reciprocity in 1911. But, presto chango, we find him going down to Washington to try to consummate a treaty, with the words "no truck or trade with the Yankees " still echoing throughout the country.
That brings us up to the 1935 election. I think I shall have to confess that I was just as rabid in my determination to get lower tariffs for the west as were my opponents to get higher tariffs. Looking backward I do not think we went about it in the right way at all. How can we expect a minority in the west to overcome, overpower and overdominate the great industrial majority in the east? It is not democratic. At all events, it is not representative government and in my estimation it is not the right way to go about it. In the last sixty years, as the result of these periodical battles we entered into with such ardour, what have we got but a lot of turmoil and a lot of good time spent-worse than wasted-and a great deal of ill feeling engendered between the east and the west? In the end we got very little, anyway, that remained permanent.
I believe the Minister of Finance should face the fact that there are many items which still bear duties from twenty-five per cent to forty-five per cent, and in making up his budget I would ask him to give particular attention to them. No matter how much we in the west or others in low tariff provinces have the tariff reduced, it will still be higher than we want. In other words, no common tariff has yet been devised to suit all parts of Canada, and particularly to suit the western provinces. What are we going to do or say about it?
I wish to thank the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) for using the words "compensatory adjustment" in his excellent address of yesterday. I believe they are better than the word "compensation," which I had intended to use, but they mean the same thing. We have been barking up the wrong tree in our proper efforts to get lower tariffs. Even if we get it right or nearly right, as we did in May, 1930, in the Dunning budget, the electors may take a notion that they want it up again. That is futile. I have too few years longer to live to spend them in that kind of everchanging thing. I want to try the principle of compensatory adjustment as suggested by the Minister of Labour.



The Address-Mr. Motherwell
Well, what does compensatory adjustment mean? Let us first consider my own word, compensation. When confederation was established the maritime provinces were a little leary about coming into it. They thought they were so small territorially and so small numerically, although giants in other respects, that their weight would not properly be felt in the parliament of Canada. For that, they were given a compensatory adjustment by way of larger representation in the senate. Because of the grievances they had advanced, I think there was some ground for that action. But what I want to bring out is this, that whether the principle was right or wrong, it was endorsed and applied.
Then later, when the new prairie provinces came into existence, inasmuch as we had no debt-that would be a fine thing to be able to say to-day-a special grant was given to us in lieu of debt, to put us on a basis of equality with the other provinces. As may be recalled, the original four provinces absorbed the provincial debts of those respective provinces. The western provinces coming in, and having no debt, were, as already indicated, given grants in lieu of debt. There is the principle of compensation, and it has been recognized ever since.
Later on the Conservative party of 1931, which I thought was at that time doing everything in the worst way possible, adopted the policy of compensation through the five cent bonus on wheat. I believe, at least, that the idea was that of compensation. By that compensatory provision they gave about $12,000,000 in bonuses to farmers who needed it least; I never knew how they compensated the poor fellows who had no crops. Those moneys were paid entirely on a bushelage rather than an acreage basis.
I believe however that I am wandering away from my point. It is that the principle of compensation has been recognized by all parties since confederation. It must be recognized in our homes and our respective occupations. Not a day passes but what some kind of compromise or compensation is made everywhere, from the state right down to the honest peasant in his home. There would be no such thing as living peaceably together unless there was a great measure of compromise and compensation.
I do not need to elaborate upon the soundness of the principle. One must wonder, however, how it will work out. As the Minister of Labour pointed out in his memorandum, what are we going to get in lieu of the high tariffs? Certain injustices are bound to arise in a high tariff policy imposed upon rural Canada. Do we wish to keep the provinces suffering in perpetuity those injustices in that

condition, or are we going to respond to the disciplining effect of the times in which we are living, when the international situation seems bent on self-destruction, and when the whole world may be thrown into the vortex of war in the twinkling of an eye.
The dogs of war may be unleashed at a moment's notice. I do not wish to anticipate it, but we must remember that we ought to be in the best possible shape to meet the worst which may develop. We ought not to be caught unprepared. The way to be prepared is to look after our own home affairs; we ought to have them working as harmoniously as possible, and not go into war in the midst of national turmoil at home, as we did the last time in 1914. It is bad enough to go into it, and in all conscience I hope we may never have to, but let us anticipate possibilities. I am not making these statements because I happen to belong to the party in power; as a matter of fact, sometimes I would like to be in the opposition for just a few minutes. I am not pleading for conciliation or toleration because I fear that somebody will attack the government; not at all; but it is better for the state and for everybody that we should live as harmoniously as possible during these perilous times. This method of lowering and raising tariffs is sometimes called scientific, but it is nothing of the kind. It is based largely on the exigencies of the occasion. I say that we should not waste our energies in the manner I have described. What kind of compensation do I refer to? What are we to get in lieu of this high tariff that has been imposed on us during all these years? Before entering on that, may I condense into a few short sentences what I have tried to say in a somewhat rambling manner?
Every legitimate and reasonable effort should be made to reduce the customs tariff, particularly on the implements of production, consistent with revenue requirements. So long as the middle west's interests continue to be largely agricultural and its representation in parliament so relatively small, and the central east so largely industrial and its representation in parliament so relatively large, no common tariff can be devised that will satisfy both, if we are to preserve the principle of majority rule and representative government. On the other hand, neither should the majority impose upon the minority in Canada a high protective tariff that has been so burdensome to agriculture, particularly in the prairie west, as to cause constantly growing feelings of resentment against such transparent injustice. While our customs tariffs have varied in height from time to

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
time, depending upon which party was in power, no tariff has yet been devised that has proven satisfactory to the middle prairie west, nor is it likely to be in the immediate future unless some method of compensation for losses sustained by such minority already alluded to be adopted and put into equitable operation.
Now I will give the house what I have in mind, and I am giving only my own thoughts; I do not represent anybody except my constituents, and I am not sure that I represent them all the time, because when I talk about compensation, their idea may be to keep on fighting wildcats all the time. At my years I am just a little bit out of that class; but I intend to persevere, first, in getting the tariff down as low as possible by every reasonable and honourable means, and then let us make up for the deficiency by some form of compensation. I have two suggestions in that regard. First, we want, not a wheat board, but a grain board. We want one that is selfsustaining and non-hibernating, if you can guess what kind that is, and the implications involved. I use that word so that a lot of people will have to look up their dictionary. I repeat that the grain board should be selfsustaining and non-hibernating. This is not the appropriate time, I realize, to go into the grain marketing problem, because we have a competent and capable commission studying that question and the country is now anxiously awaiting its report. Pending its arrival I shall have to pass on, somewhat regretfully, to the other compensation that I have in mind!
Shortly after the west began to be settled in the early days-that is, exclusive of the old Selkirk settlement and the settlement around Portage la Prairie-the Hudson Bay railway became a live issue. Cruel people say that it always was used as an election football. Well, maybe it was. Those forty miles of rails that ran north of Winnipeg never got us anywhere, except that they were to somebody's advantage-I do not know whose. But it was a live issue all through the years since 1880. We were just like other countries similarly situated. There is a feeling in the breast of every nation that makes them seek the shortest route to the sea. That was the case long years ago, long before Solomon, whether it was by caravans over the desert or by the seven seas. There has always been that inherent instinct in the human breast to reach the seaboard by the shortest and safest possible route. That is what we were desirous of in the west, but it took us a long while to attain it, until at last Sir Wilfrid Laurier, coming back from a trip in the west, was again prepared to make
the sacrifice largely for the west, because naturally there was not much love for it displayed in the east.
In the city of Hamilton in 1908 Sir Wilfrid Laurier pledged his party to tire construction of the Hudson Bay railway. Then the matter hung fire for a while, but not long afterwards the bridge over The Pas was under construction when a change of government took place. Contracts were let to a point called Split Lake for the construction of the road, and then again we had a change of government at a critical time. But the new government carried on the construction of the road, and headed it for Port Nelson. I am not going to enter into the old story of how the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), then Minister of Railways, in a most expeditious way, as soon as he got the report of Sir Frederick Palmer, changed the terminus from Port Nelson to Fort Churchill. There you have a real port. I do not know for sure who it was that had blundered in choosing Port Nelson, but I know that the whole undertaking was pretty nearly ruined and would have been ruined if the road had run into Port Nelson. Well, we now have this port at Fort Churchill, and it is not doing very much. How could you expect it to do much at the beginning, when the insurance rate on the Hudson Bay route was eight times as much as on the St. Lawrence route? You could not expect traffic to seek the Hudson Bay outlet with such an enormous handicap in the matter of marine insurance.
And there was always something happening to injure the route. We know the story of the Bright Fan and its drunken shipmaster. That was all brought out in evidence. I do not know whether he ever got a certificate again for running a boat across the Atlantic, but he never should have received a certificate in the first place to shipmaster a boat through the, to him, strange waters of Hudson strait, where people's lives and property, and the reputation of the route were at stake.
But now we have the Hudson Bay railway; we have a good roadbed; we have a good port, and we have a good elevator. Of course, with our restricted crops, the traffic must be meagre for some time, but I was wondering if we could not get some kind of move on in anticipation of better crops. One of the difficulties with the Hudson Bay route, we are told, is the short open season, and that is one of the difficulties; but so far as good water is concerned and so far as safety is concerned, many shipmasters who have taken cargoes of wheat out of Fort Churchill declare that it is just as safe a route as any other in Canada with seasonal ports. I
The Address-Mr. Motherwell

am not a nautical authority at all, and I do not pretend to be ; but I know that good water, lots of depth and width, is absolutely necessary to successful navigation, and I know that Captain Bernier gave evidence before the grain commission in 1925 in the province of Quebec with respect to his experience on this route. I have not a copy of his evidence with me, but if anybody wants further information on the matter, any member of that grain commission, and particularly the chairman thereof, will be able to confirm everything I say regarding Captain Bernier's evidence.
He was master, or second master, of a ship when he was only seventeen years of age, and he traversed those northern waters almost continuously in the employ of the government until he was seventy-five years old. I had the privilege of meeting him here in the Chateau Laurier about four or five years ago, when we went all over this evidence that he gave, and he reported that he was more than ever firmly convinced that what I am going to mention would be the proper course to pursue. The present period is too short for the route to be open to provide it with a sufficient volume of business, and without volume hardly any business can be profitable. You cannot grow one acre or even twenty acres of wheat and equip yourself with machinery and make the operation pay. So it is with this new outlet; we must get the volume in order to do a reasonable proportion of the business which will be available when our crops come back, as they will do sooner or later.
Captain Bernier testified before the grain commission in 1925 in the province of Quebec, and took the ground that not only was this a possible route, a workable route, but that it had a great future, and that the proper port was Churchill. Not only that, but he observed that the greatest handicap would be the shortness of the season, and he advocated that the government provide the necessary boat equipment, strengthen and reinforce it, to take care of new ice conditions in those northern waters. As hon. members know, when the ice is forming in the fall of the year, Fort Churchill can be kept open two weeks later by Ihe use of a boat that would not be called an ice-breaker but could open up the way during at least the formation of ice in the early fall and at the same time could be used for transporting grain. I am not an authority; I am quoting Captain Bernier, who said that a number of suitable reinforced boats which would stand considerable pressure of ice could be used for transporting wheat and at the same time for keeping that route open .two weeks earlier in the spring and two weeks
IMr. Motherwell.]
later in the fall. That makes a month and would give us a maximum period of four months' safe transportation over that route to the world's markets. This evidence was taken a long while ago-thirteen years-and I have scarcely heard of it since. I do not wish to magnify anything I have done, but I think I did contribute a little towards getting that route built to the right port.

Alone I certainly could not have done it. I do not know whether my good friend and old colleague wishes me to extol him for the masterly part he played in a crisis, but I can assure him the people of the west give him full credit for it. One way to compensate us would be to see whether somehow or another that period of safe navigation could be lengthened. As far as I know there has been no attempt to do this. We have suitable direction-finding stations established, and if these shores were lighted and appropriately equipped as those of the St. Lawrence, this would add considerably to the safety of the route. I admit freely that considerable progress has been made in the above direction, but now is the time to consider whether that route is built for ornamental purposes or for practical use. I think decidedly it could be made fit for practical use. I do not like to suggest any expenditures at this time, but the subject should be carefully studied. Look up and study Captain Bernier's report. If you cannot get it, consult the chairman of the commission before whom his evidence was taken. Possibly the report is in the archives of the university of Saskatchewan. Governments cannot keep all these volumes of evidence indefinitely, but we will try to find it.
I hope that our eastern friends, who naturally are interested in eastern ports, will consider the question we have been discussing. A member of the government has suggested that we have "compensating adjustments." Will hon. members adjust their views regarding this matter and permit us to have the natural, inherent instincts of the human breast gratified by reaching tidewater with our exports as quickly and as safely as possible. That is one of the long heart's desires of the west. Alberta is not much interested, if at all. British Columbia had not always the Panama canal; it had not always the Crows-nest pass rates extended to the Pacific. I think fellow Canadians from other parts of Canada can join with us and be tolerant of our little ambitions and nostrums-if you like to call them that. The Hudson Bay railway is a reality. We have now to see whether we can

The Address-Mr. Lawson
make some practical use of it, and this is the way I respectfully suggest that it should be gone about.
I believe I have covered what I wanted to say at present; in any case my forty minutes are almost up. There are a number of other problems I should like to speak about, but they will be more properly said later in the session, after the various reports have been tabled.
Hon. J. EARL LAWSON (York South) It is not my purpose this afternoon to discuss fiscal policy, so I shall not attempt to follow the remarks of the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) but rather devote my attention to those of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe).
When the Minister of Transport started his address this afternoon I came to the conclusion, after his first few sentences, that he was performing the painful duty of answering for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the House of Commons; but before he finished he left no doubt in my mind that he as a responsible minister of the government was approving their actions and approving their recommendations that the licence fee should be increased from S2 to $2.50 per annum, and that each individual radio should be licensed. The minister pointed out that the two bills previously passed in the house in connection with radio broadcasting were passed by a unanimous vote. Lest the impression should have been left that those of us who did not vote against the measure therefore spontaneously approved it, I should point out that we who did not agree in all its details with that measure merely followed the unanimous recommendation of a committee of the house, which recommendation, for reasons that I shall state in a moment and that were then presented to the house, we did not see fit to oppose.
The minister said this afternoon that he was willing to pay for three radio licences at the increased rate. Possibly he and I can well afford to do so, 'but that does not lend any weight to the argument on this question. The vast majority of radios in this country are owned by people whose incomes are so meagre that it is a burden to pay $2, much less S2.50 for a radio licence.
I want to make it clear at the outset that the present Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not the tribunal which was set up by the original radio act passed by the former government in 1932. That was all scrapped with the advent of the Liberal party in 1936.

speechtext:
The legislation was introduced in 1936. The advent of the Liberal party was in 1935, but so far as this house was concerned the government introduced its legislation in the session of 1936, and the present act is their responsibility. The present Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was set up by this government.
No law is any better than its administration, and where the administration of a law does not work for the benefit of the people of Canada, then, under our democratic system, the responsibility devolves upon the government of bringing in a measure to change that law. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps), who spoke this afternoon, expressed a view that, coming from him, was rather a surprise to me, to the effect that he had a suspicion that those who opposed the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its activities had some interest or ulterior motive. Let me say to him that I have no financial interest of any kind in any radio station, in any magazine, in any newspaper, in any interest that conflicts with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, nor in my professional practice have I any client who has such an interest.
The minister spoke of the committees which heard evidence on radio broadcasting prior to 1932. How well I remember the one that was not a parliamentary committee. Prior to 1932 a committee was set up, and represented upon it were the business element, the church element, the labour element, charitable and philanthropic societies, every phase of Canadian activity. That committee made a recommendation in favour of the nationalization of the radio. But why? With the object primarily of promoting Canadian unity. We in this house were told that the Americanization of this dominion by United States programs was the dominant factor behind the decision of the committee and of the parliament of that day to bring in a broadcasting act, and that another primary purpose was to develop in Canada all the varied resources of radio entertainment, in other words, that we might develop Canadian talent. We were to provide work for Canadian musicians, Canadian playwrights, Canadian actors, Canadian singers and Canadian technicians. Any members who were in the house at the time will remember that we were to limit advertising. We were told that it was this advertising which was so reprehensible to Canadian listeners, and all this boon we were to receive for the small sum of $1 per licence.
The radio commission was established in 1932 and struggled during its existence to improve Canadian programs, and I am not going
The Address-Mr. Lawson

to suggest that that commission or the one which is now in existence has not made some improvement in Canadian programs. I remember that one of the early acts of the old ' radio commission was to limit advertising on the air to the maximum of five minutes to the hour. Well, we had the advent of this new Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in 1936. We were told that in accomplishing our purpose it was going to be far superior to the old commission. It was to have a board of governors, upon which there were to be astute business men, and it was to be representative of all phases of Canadian activity. A new era was to dawn. After two years it has dawned, and it has dawned with a huge increase in United States advertising.
I have spoken of the representations made in this parliament as to the Americanization of Canada through the penetration of United States advertising. The minister in his speech to-day repeated the figures given by the chairman of the broadcasting corporation when he delivered an address a while ago in which he told us about the number of hours-eight and three-quarters out of ninety-eight-that were given up to United States advertising. He said:
Advertising programs originating in the United States occupied eight and three-quarter hours of the ninety-eight hours broadcast weekly over the CBC network.
I do not know whether that gentleman, and the minister this afternoon, intended to create the impression, by that statement which has gone abroad, that eight and three-quarter hours constituted the only United States programs we were receiving, because what he meant and what the minister meant was that out of ninety-eight hours the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation were being paid for only eight and three-quarter hours of United States programs. If you take the very schedule produced by the chairman you will find that the total United States programs, in whatever week he took, amounted to twenty-six and one-quarter hours out of ninety-eight hours of broadcasting. Bear in mind that I am speaking now of the penetration of Canada, of the Americanization of Canada by United States programs. I quite agree with the minister that music is international, and unfortunately, not being on the investigating committee, I have no means of access to the records of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I have some familiarity only with the station in the neighbourhood from which I come. But hon. members will notice that when I asked the minister this afternoon as to the number of hours of United States broadcasting we have from CBL, the new

50.000	watt station near Toronto, which gives broadcasting coverage for the whole province of Ontario. I found that there was thirty-five per cent of commercial broadcasting, eighteen per cent of which is commercial United States broadcasting, which the minister explained meant paid advertising. I could not do anything with the figures he mentioned, because I do not know the week to which they relate.
The radio corporation sends out a bulletin issued in advance showing its programs for each week, and I took the trouble to have made, from the bulletin they turned out for this week, commencing with February 6, a chart which I now show to the members of the house. Every space marked in red on the chart is broadcasting in Canada by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation of a program originating in the United States. What proportion of them is paid advertising I have no means of ascertaining without having access to the records of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
The minister says that the total radio broadcasting by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is ninety-eight hours. That again may apply to chain broadcasting. I am referring to CBL. But bear in mind that when I refer to CBL I am dealing with one-third of the population of Canada-I shall prove that before I finish. According to the bulletin turned out by the broadcasting corporation, from which that chart is computed, of 112J broadcasting hours during this very week, 48 hours are occupied by United States programs. Again I cannot say what proportion is United States paid advertising. Now percentages sometimes are deceptive. When the minister tells us that eighteen per cent of the time of CBL is taken up with United States advertising programs that does not give a correct picture, because we must bear in mind that the most advantageous hours of broadcasting are recognized to be from eight a.m. to eleven a.m. and six p.m. to eleven p.m., with the exception of Saturday night. Let me turn back to that same chart, so that the house may have a picture of the position from eight a.m. to eleven a.m. every day of this week, everything shown in red being United States programs. The result is that on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, you have one hour of Canadian programs between eight a.m. and eleven a.m., and on Saturday only half an hour.

speechtext: Are the hours between eight a.m. and eleven a.m. the advantageous hours spoken of?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: So I am told by broadcasters.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is very interesting.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The largest audience is reached between eight a.m. and eleven a.m. except the audience reached between six p.m. and eleven p.m.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I wish you were our salesman to sell that time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Apparently the corporation is not having any difficulty in selling it, in view of the cut rates. I shall come to that before I finish. Now, referring to the hours between six p.m. and eleven pm., the choicest hours of all with the exception of Saturday night, by observing that chart one will see that there are more United States programs than Canadian programs during those hours. With what result? With this result, that as the greatest number of listeners are reached between the hours I mentioned, the Canadian-sponsored broadcasts can be had only at the off hours, and the consequence of that is that the entertainers engaged for Canadian-sponsored programs receive small pay. In fact the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation pays singers and entertainers for broadcast programs |5, $7.50 and $10 per performance. Is that the encouragement we were told was to be given to Canadian talent in this country? The minister mentioned Sir Ernest MacMillan. Sir Ernest MacMillan heads one of the finest musical organizations in the country, the Toronto Symphony Orchestra, an orchestra which is maintained in large measure by public subscription, and which, in order to exist, has employed some of the finest musicians in this country at salaries so meagre that hon. members would find them incredible. Sir Ernest MacMillan was considered such a great Canadian musician and composer that he was knighted by His Majesty the King. May I ask why we have never had the Toronto Symphony Orchestra broadcast by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as a sustaining program? If Canadians are anxious to listen to Sir Ernest MacMillan leading the New York Philharmonic Orchestra, how much better it would be if Americans were listening to Sir Ernest MacMillan leading his own symphony orchestra in Canada. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) spoke of the joy he had in hearing the opening of the United States congress. I sincerely hope he was able to hear it through to the end, because I was listening to a broadcast of
His Excellency the Governor General of Canada addressing the Scottish curlers when they were here, and it was cut off in the middle in order to bring on the Packard Motor Car program from the United States.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member is entirely wrong.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
