subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Read it now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am not going to read it now because I have much more important things to say than reading a statute at this moment. This is the development of Canadian talent and Canadian ideals which we are getting from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; this is the policy for which we are asked to pay increased licence fees. To those who may be labouring under the belief that programs now being heard are of an essentially educational and inspirational nature, designed to create and inspire a clearer concept of Canadian ideals, one has but to listen to the programs broadcast from time to time. It may be that there are those who like blackface comedians and Charlie McCarthy and the Stroud twins; I listen to it myself. Like the Minister of Transport and the Board of Governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, those who wish can now get a twenty-inch high cardboard facsimile of the dummy Charlie McCarthy by buying four pounds of dated coffee and sending in the coupons.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Have you any objection?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I think we may well ask in all seriousness what educational programs, what rich incidents of Canadian historical drama, what cultural aspects of Canadian life, what encouragement to Canadian practitioners of the arts have found a place in the program planning of the great Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? Make no mistake, I am not objecting to the broadcasting as sustaining programs of Charlie McCarthy or United States programs of any kind. But I am objecting to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation prostituting the purposes for which it was created by statute and charging the Canadian listeners increased licence fees for doing it, while our United States cousins can listen to it all and pay not a cent for it. That is the thing to which I am objecting.
Now I said I would come back to advertising. I said that formerly the Canadian radio commission placed a maximum limit on advertising of five minutes to the hour. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation when it came into power immediately doubled the maximum, making it ten minutes to the hour. Then recently they brought in a new policy, which is to solicit and sell to United States advertisers broadcasting time over our air channels in competition with the private stations which I again say the corporation has power to control.
Now let me come back to the chart for a moment. I stated that I had no means of knowing what percentage of the total of the United States programs was paid advertising. I have to accept the statement made by the chairman of the broadcasting corporation in this speech, in which he tells us that the revenue of the corporation from this source for this fiscal year will be about $400,000, and they want to reach a total of $500,000. If they are to obtain $500,000 net, Mr. Speaker, by the time they pay commissions to advertising solicitors and the different commissions paid to the stations they will have to raise at least $750,000 gross. While I am talking about paying I should like to know who paid the broadcasting corporation for this national broadcast by the chairman of that corporation? If it was paid for with the money of the people, by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, I want to know if anyone

who is opposed to the policy of that corporation, as now accepted by the minister, is going to be given an opportunity of presenting the other side of the case. If not I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that we will set up in this country a bureaucracy which ultimately will destroy this parliament if we put into the hands of any small group of men the power to broadcast their views with the cost paid by the people, raised in taxes, while they charge me $3,000 an hour for a coast to coast broadcast in order to give some picture of the other side of the question.
We are told by Mr. Brockington that he only wants advertising revenue up to $500,000 from this new scheme of selling advertising to the United States, and he says he only wants that until we are self-supporting from other sources. What are the other sources? The moment he ceases to take that advertising the only other source is the poor Canadian taxpayer who is going to have his radio licence fee increased not by fifty cents but by five dollars in order to raise the money required. Mr. Brockington says he only wants to sell this advertising until such time as he attains that happy position. That tempts me to repeat some comment I read in some paper, that it was exactly similar to a bank robber saying, "I only want two more hold-ups and then I will reform. I will have enough then with which to retire and live pleasantly for the rest of my days."
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, by the solicitation of United States advertising, is causing a serious loss to many industries in this country. There is only a fixed appropriation for advertising in Canada. That appropriation must be divided between national magazines, local magazines, weekly press, daily press, signboards and the radio. To the extent that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation participates in that advertising appropriation some other medium must lose. I believe private enterprise is willing to accept competition on an equal basis, but I say the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is using the money of the people as a subsidy to enable it to undersell private enterprise.
Let me show why I say that. In order to broadcast you have to lease wire lines. A private station leasing wire lines has to anticipate the total number of hours it is going to broadcast in any one day. Obviously it cannot get sponsored programs for the whole of the day. Therefore it has to pay wire charges for hours from which it gets no revenue. Consequently in fixing its prices

The Address-Mr. Lawson
for time on the air it has to take into account the hours during which it is using sustaining programs. The broadcasting corporation also has to lease wires for the number of hours it is going to use them during the day. But when it comes to fixing the price which it is going to charge the advertiser on a sponsored program for any hour, it does not have to make the rate as high as the private station, because the corporation says: Oh, the advertiser is paying the rate for that hour, and the money we raise from the people of Canada by taxation is paying for the other hours.
To-day the minister said there was a standard rate and that anybody could buy time on the air at that rate. I challenge that statement. I have in my hand a comparative schedule published by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the costs of each station, beside which I have the standard rate which I am asked to pay if I go to a private station. Again I will take the station I know best. CBL in Toronto. The published rate of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for one-half hour over CBL is S180. The standard rate-
Is the hon. gentleman reading the rate for CBL as part of the chain or individually?

I am reading it as part
of the chain.

Then may I point out that the hon. gentleman is comparing two things which cannot be compared. If he will read the tariff for station CBL as a single station he will have something comparable with a private station.

All right; I am only talking about the private station as a private station. I have no chain figures available. The rate for CBL, as published by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, for one-half hour is $180. The standard rate, based upon a private station cost plus five per cent, is $165. As I stand in the house at the moment making this speech there sits in the Chateau Laurier a man with a contract in his pocket for a halfhour over that station at $120 less ten per cent, less fifteen per cent. That is why I challenge the statement made by the minister this afternoon.
May I ask if that last price was for a chain broadcast or an individual broadcast?
An individual broadcast.
My hon. friend is very careless with his figures here. I hope he can substantiate them.

I seldom use figures I
cannot substantiate. Give me a committee and the opportunity to substantiate them and I shall do so.
If my hon. friend asks for it I shall give it to him now.

In connection with this
sale of United States advertising the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has established an attractive range of discounts, which pyramid as more stations are used, in order to attract that United States advertising. The Canadian stations cannot even arrange a chain of stations among themselves without going to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for approval.
I am told that within the last few weeks a dozen contracts have been signed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for choice hours, such as I outlined to-day, and the Canadian advertiser has to take what is left.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me demonstrate to the house what our United States cousins think of their new privileges over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation chain. I am sure the initials N.B.C., meaning the National Broadcasting Company, are familiar to every member of the house, since that is one of the greatest corporations in the United States. They have produced an attractive advertisement, of which I hold a photostatic copy in my hand, designed to get business from United States advertisers over Canadian stations. On the front in large white letters on a black strip we find the letters NBC. Then, opposite the letter "N" we find the letters "ow," opposite "B" we find "etter" and opposite "C" we find "overage," the whole reading "NBC, Now Better Coverage in Montreal and Toronto." Turning to the inside page we find across the top "New NBC Canadian supplementary facilities in Montreal" and "in Toronto."
CBC?

No, this is NBC. Then they go on in these words:
Two major Canadian radio stations, CBM and CBF, in Montreal, joined NBC networks on November 14, 1937.
Then further down:
CBF:	French-language station, full time,
50,000 watts, clear channel, 910 kilocycles, owned by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, is available (alone, or in combination with CBM or CFCF) to advertisers using either the basic blue or the basic red network.
The Address-Mr. Lawson

Then, the next paragraph refers to Ontario:
NBC service in Ontario has just taken a big step forward. Station CRCT, NBC affiliate in Toronto, has increased its power-
And so on. Then they go on to say:
This is a clear-ehannel, full-time station operating on a frequency of 840 kilocycles. It is owned by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Then, on both sides I find notices as to the market, and it is stated that by using the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's station in Toronto one may reach the province of Ontario, with thirty-three per cent of the population of Canada, and that by using the station in Montreal one reaches twenty-seven per cent of the population. In other words, by using these two supplementaries to the national broadcasting chain the broadcaster reaches sixty per cent of the population of Canada-and the people of Canada have just paid, out of their licence fees to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, for completing these two new 50,000 watt stations.
What is the result of all this? The result is unemployment.
Oh, oh.

Yes, more unemployment to Canadian singers, Canadian musicians and Canadian technicians. Every time we take business from magazines and newspapers, by broadcasting United States advertising, we are putting printers, typesetters and other workers out of jobs. May I say to the hon. gentlemen who just said "Oh, oh," that that was not my expression. I am simply repeating a resolution passed in Toronto by the Trades and Labour Council. That resolution was passed within the last week, and published in the newspapers.
For the privilege of maintaining the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, created by this Liberal government, and maintaining the policies I have outlined, several branches of Canadian industry must be taxed to subsidize unfair competition with themselves; Canadian radio owners are being compelled to pay increased licence fees. I protest. On behalf of those associated with me in the Conservative ranks in the House of Commons, who have not yet had an opportunity to speak for themselves, I protest. On behalf of the people I represent in this chamber, I protest.
I promised the hon. member I would read the statute. If you will permit me, Mr. Speaker. I should like to be given an opportunity to lay my hand on the section stating that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has control over private stations. I am sorry

that in the short time at my disposal I cannot put my hand upon it, but if hon. members interested-
Because it is not there.

-will read chapter 24 of the statutes for 1936 they will find set out the power and control held by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation over private stations. If I might cite one instance of control, may I ask who it was that imposed the censorship about which I complained last year? Was it a private station or was it the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? If they cannot control what was broadcast over a private station, how do they censor the programs which go upon the air?
Because the act gives them that privilege, but it does not give them the privilege to say how private stations shall run their programs.
I did not suggest that.

What the hon. member stated is not the fact; why not say so?
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, as I sat in the house when it opened at eight o'clock I was of opinion for a little while, when I saw so few members present, that my remarks this evening might take the form of a rather intimate conversation between yourself and myself, but I am happy to note now that the house is not quite so sparse as I thought for a moment it was going to be.
I regret that the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) is not in his seat at present because, with most of the other members of the house, I listened before the dinner recess with a great deal of interest to what he had to say. I felt that whatever his case was with respect to radio he was certainly presenting it very well, perhaps making the best of a bad case, but at all events presenting his ideas with some force. That aspect of radio criticism which has to do with, shall I say, the permeation of Canada with American ideas is one which interests me particularly, and I recall that the hon. member for York South did not seem to fear nearly so greatly the permeation of Canada with American ideas when he was the sponsor, if I remember correctly, of the "Mr. Sage" campaign which was carried on in 1935. Apparently in 1935

The Address-Mr. Maybank
the belief must have existed, as I have said once before in the house, that the Canadian people were hardy enough to stand any such onslaught on their national thought and life; but apparently the situation is a little bit different now. At that time I remember we were a little afraid that the Conservative party had gone Yankee, but I was glad to note from the way the hon. member spoke this afternoon that if he ever had any such intentions he has recanted, retraced his steps, and is now facing in the other direction.
I also regret the absence from the house at the moment of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) because, in common with most hon. members, I listened the other day with considerable interest to his offering, if we might call it that, in this debate. During the recess we have all had an opportunity of noting in the various journals of the country that, what they were pleased to call the political truce existing between the leader of the opposition and the government, was going to come to an end, and we have all been on the qui vive to observe what would be the form of behaviour of the leader of the opposition in signalizing the end of that truce. It may have been observed that these journals to which I have referred made no mention, in speaking of the truce, and the ending of the truce, of the right hon. gentleman's party. Rather it was always said that the truce which "the leader of the opposition" had permitted to continue would come to an end. All these journals realized, in their references to the great Conservative party, that He was It, and It was He; that all the members of that party were comprehended in the term, "the leader of the party"-all except its organizer, who, it seems, will not go to work until the party gets a new leader.
We have now had an opportunity of observing the manner in which the truce came to an end. We have heard the theme song, one might say, of the right hon. leader of the opposition in the new play that he proposes to enact in Canada. I read over his speech very carefully, and I think most people will agree that, aside from captious criticism, from what in the language of the street we call just mud-slinging, there was very little in the speech at all. The theme song of 1930 was "Promises" and the play was entitled, "A pledge for every Parish." That yields place now to this new opera.
Very soon after commencing and being rude to a new member of the house, after first misrepresenting what that hon. member had said, we found the leader of the opposition going on to discuss the actions of the
Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as though the Prime Minister had been a Roosevelt agent, or at any rate he allowed that inference to be drawn.
Then we had this great hint of corruption. That is the second offering we have for 1938 -the hint of corruption-but so far the fear of making direct charges has restrained him.
There was also an attempt to make capital out of imaginary grievances supposed to exist somewhere in the cabinet, when such difficulties do not apparently exist at all.
Next we had an attack made upon men who are earnestly engaged in an important task throughout Canada, the important task of trying to lay the groundwork for greater unity and a greater degree of harmony in this country, something we all have known for a long time was necessary if this dominion was to endure. It would seem almost as if the leader of the opposition was afraid something was going to be accomplished. It would seem as if he wanted to render nugatory the work that any person else might attempt. The work of that royal commission was misrepresented. Surely it was a misrepresentation to suggest that its business was to amend the constitution of Canada. That was his suggestion. Indeed the words he used very clearly stated that the commission was engaged in amending the constitution, when as a matter of fact there is in the terms of reference to that commission no foundation whatever for any such suggestion. But it would seem that to state the case thus would engender fear in the country. It would seem as though, adopting the words of the speech from the throne-"the strains and stresses" of confederation-he had taken for his motto:	If
there are not enough strains and stresses in this confederation now, I will put in a few more.
Then there was his attempt to turn the east against the west, and city against city, saying that certain things had been promised in the St. Henry by-election, and that if Montreal can get such and such a promise why cannot Calgary get it, why cannot Vancouver get it, why not Edmonton, why not Winnipeg? But when you come to look at that a little more carefully, you will find that they can get that promise, that they have had that promise. It has been implicit all along in all relief arrangements, that what was indicated in the St. Henry by-election had been the order of the day in all these other places. As the right hon. gentleman puts it himself, it was said: "If local government fails, the central government will not fail". That, Mr. Speaker, has always been understood, and there has never been any
2G8
The Address-Mr. Maybank

difficulty about it. The only difficulty there has been was whether or not the local governments would get 'to the point of admitting complete failure.
The real difficulty about relief is not that. The difficulty we have here in the matter of sharing relief costs is, in my opinion, that the central government has never taken its full share, the share it should have taken, of this relief expense. But at that, the present handling of the relief problem is immeasurably superior to what it was over the five long years between 1930 and 1935. We have here, however, an attempt to set one section of the country against another by suggesting that one section can get what another section cannot. That, decidedly, is not the case, but it apparently suits the right hon. gentleman's convenience to speak that way. I would not say that he is malevolent, that he definitely wishes ill but his approach to this particular problem could hardly be different if he were malevolent. He would create two stresses where there was only one before, and two strains where there had been only one.
I wish also to put on record again, what most likely all have noticed, his misrepresentation of the position of Canada in the money market. It was said that the position of Canada was inferior to that of Australia, and facts were given to bear out this conclusion. A comparison of an Australian loan with a Canadian loan was made. Of course we know that what was stated was not true. Next day the inaccuracy of these remarks was exposed. Then, if nothing else had occurred, it would be our business to consider whether the right hon. gentleman knew of the untruth at the time he stated it. He tells us, however, that he had in mind a former loan of Australia, that he got the facts respecting it and then compared that former loan with one of the Dominion of Canada which was a current loan, and, thus endeavouring to compare things which were not comparable, he concluded that Canada's position in the money market was inferior to that of Australia. Since he asks us to believe that is what he did, of course there is not any question about its being believed. But if a little more care had been taken, the critique in his main speech would not have gone out to the country in the way it did; and when you publish a statement throughout the country, any amount of explanation afterwards will never quite overtake the misrepresentation originally made.
I remember a story about a clergyman who, being slandered, went to the woman who had slandered him, and explained the situation to her. She promptly accepted the explanation

and made an apology. But he conducted her to a high place and gave her a cushion or a pillow or a bag of feathers and asked her to scatter the contents about. This she did, and he then said to her, "Now just put them back in the bag." Of course she could not do it. The clergyman realized that no further explanation was needed to demonstrate to her the impossibility of catching up with a false statement when it had once been made. In this particular case we have, either a deliberate attempt-and that must be ruled out-to misrepresent the position of Canada, or negligence in the discovery and presentation of facts; consequently there is a misrepresentation of Canada's position, and so the situation is just as bad as if it had been deliberate.
In going over the speech of the leader of this once great party I find in it only one concrete statement of political philosophy, and that, it would seem, is just a little bit more absurd than any other declaration he has ever made. That was the declaration that free trade makes for war. I do not propose at the moment to pursue the general idea of tariff making and the philosophy underlying tariffs, because I believe there will be plenty of opportunity at a later time. But I wish to remark at this time that this question of high tariff and low tariff should not be regarded as an east versus west proposition. It seems to me that the concept which better pictures this problem is that of primary producers paying by way of taxes and higher prices for processes; it is the concept of the primary producer versus the processor. Perhaps, in view of the fact that the proportion of primary producers in western Canada is larger some people there get into the habit of looking upon this particular controversy as one of west versus east. But I think we should not allow ourselves to fall into that error, because decidedly it is not the true nature of the issue.
But revert for a moment to the "Free Trade Brings War" doctrine. Here you have it that Peel and Canning caused the Crimean war when they reduced duties on a large number of articles, and particularly when, after Canning's death, Peel became in favour of the repeal of the Corn Laws and brought about almost complete free trade. As a matter of fact the right hon. gentleman, I believe, particularly mentioned the Crimean war and related i't to these particular acts of these English statesmen. So all British wars thereafter up to the time of the great war appear to have been caused, on this theory, by the free trade policy of Great Britain. And further, in view of the fact that no nation in the world except Great Britain practised free

The Address-Mr. Maybank
trade before the great war, the responsibility for that war must also rest almost entirely upon the shoulders of Great Britain. That is the doctrine of the right hon. gentleman. It is a proposition so absurd that one wonders how his mouth could have framed the words.
A few years ago, when he went to England and endeavoured to persuade them to adopt a protective policy his speeches were denominated by a member of the British cabinet, and have been known from that time until now, as the "Humbug" speeches. Apparently, although Jimmie Thomas called his talk "Humbug," what the right hon. gentleman was really doing, was persuading the people of Great Britain to become peaceful and to adopt protection, for to adopt protection would be the same thing as to turn their faces in the direction of peace. Also, since the world war, when economic nationalism seems to have run riot, the fact that every nation in the world has gone in for protection to a greater or less degree is apparently the reason why the world has been so peaceful. After the nations adopted the policies of the leader of the once great Conservative party peace descended upon the world, not exactly like a dove but more like a flock of bats. I do not suppose the world has ever had a worse time from the standpoint of peace and war than in the years since the treaty of Versailles.
There is the only concrete proposition that has been laid before the house by the leader of the opposition in his lengthy speech. We have some criticism; we have harmful criticism ; we have stress creating criticism; we have strain creating criticism; and conjoined with these we have the one proposition that if you do not go in for more and more protection you are likely to be drawn into war. There we have his whole contribution, and I wish to make record of it in the house at this time in order that there may be no mistake about it.
As for myself, I wish to introduce one or two declarations I have to make with reference to the speech from the throne by asserting again, as I have often asserted before, that I do not belong to any party of a fascist or communistic nature and that I do not rest under any iron heel of discipline. Nor, since we are talking about political parties, do I answer to the crack of any party whip; in fact, I have never heard of any whip to the crack of which anyone else had to answer. I work and do my thinking in the genial warmth of the Liberal party, in which there is freedom of expression, freedom of expression as in Tennyson's England, where a man might speak the thing he would.
I realize that I am often impatient, but I believe that in the long run greater advancement will be made by working from within the party where one can find kindred spirits, than by any other means. Greater progress has been made in that way in the past, and that will hold true in the future. Of my friends who are called left-wingers, I often think that if one-tenth of the energy they devote to the organization of more extreme party forms were spent in working with, shall I say, the more impatient ones within the Liberal party, ten times more progress could be made than by the method they are pursuing. However, I have no wish to push my own ideas down anyone else's throat; everyone has his own way of working.
I propose, as my conscience from time to time directs me, to express any thoughts that occur to me, whether they are completely in consonance with the ideas of my party, or to express views not yet having gained status by an ex cathedra utterance. I feel that in doing so I would not be in any way like the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Hyndman) who, a few days ago, when he expressed willingness to see factories in Windsor and Oshawa closed, butted his revered and honoured leader in the stomach-metaphorically speaking, of course. The right hon. gentleman must have been astounded by that blow.
It is sometimes said that the government does not move fast enough, and we have before us at the present time an amendment to that effect. As I have already indicated, I have a fellow feeling with healthy impatience; but there are two points to be noted in that connection, and they stand out in bold relief. In the first place, you cannot very well say about the government that it is not doing this and that; that it is not advancing this and that measure, and every other proposal put up to it, and at the same time accuse it of being a mere vote-catching administration. You cannot have it both ways. The second point that stands out is this. When you bear in mind the tremendous increase in the mortgage debt of Canada which was incurred in the last five years before this government took hold, an increase approaching a thousand millions of dollars, you are bound to realize that, with the extra burden thus imposed, many plans which one would desire to attempt-[DOT] costly plans-cannot be immediately proceeded with. And I say that, in spite of the fact that I myself am impatient. I think, however, that when people are impatient they should try to cool themselves so as to be just.
Personally I regret the absence from the speech from the throne of any specific reference to the question of aid to low cost hous-
The Address-Mr. Maybank

ing plans. I realize that this may not mean its exclusion, and no doubt a further opportunity will be afforded to deal with the matter. I should like to observe, however, that assistance to the construction industry, which seems to be about the most depressed of all, would break the back of unemployment, and I hope to see something of that sort introduced into the house.
I welcome the references which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has made to the padlock law of Quebec. I must say candidly that if statutes are to be disallowed, I believe that statute should be disallowed. I apologize for not having said so last year; I should have made that statement then. I feel very strongly about this matter. I believe that if any statute should be disallowed, that one should be; it should not be allowed to stand. The reason I did not express this opinion last year was that I thought the law would be a dead letter. I was wrong, and I now endeavour to make amends for my failure on that occasion. Mind you, I am in favour of all necessary safeguards against subversive action, but they must be safeguards and they must be necessary.
Turning for a moment from that subject, may I say how welcome to me is the reference in the speech from the throne to unemployment insurance. I am not one of those who expect too muCh from any statute of that sort. I believe it is probably only one of the steps that will have to be taken in an endeavour to end this scourge of unemployment. No laws that we can enact could be perfect, and I should expect that any law would have to be amended almost as soon as it became operative. I certainly commend the wisdom of seeking to obtain .provincial approval of any such amendment, but I hope that lack of complete provincial approval will not hold up the address of this parliament to the British parliament asking for the amendment of the British North America Act, because it would seem to me that we must get the law operating soon, in order that we may acquire the experience necessary for further advance in an endeavour to wipe out what seems so far at any rate to be an inherent defect in the system under which we live.
I am glad to see this unemployment insurance proposal for another reason, namely that it marks the adoption of the principle of greater responsibility of the central government in respect to unemployment. I should have been glad if that principle had been adopted a little more definitely with reference to the relief difficulties that we have had in Canada for the last several years. Last year I had an opportunity of saying to the house something about the plight of the cities and

the heavy load they are made to carry. I feel that the division of the cost of unemployment relief which results in putting more than one-third upon communities which can obtain money only by direct taxation, and that upon a very narrow base, mainly real estate, is not fair. I am not saying for a moment that I believe the central government should carry the whole burden, but I say that when a division is made which results in a city such as that from which I come being forced at certain times to carry well up to fifty per cent of the total load, that division is not fair. At the present time my city is being forced to find somewhere in the neighbourhood of
SI,500,000	for this year, with all avenues of taxation already exhausted-a well nigh impossible task. I suppose there will be not more than 30,000 people upon whom the necessary levy can be made in order to obtain that large sum of money. The situation in Regina, Vancouver, Edmonton, Saskatoon and most other cities is substantially the same, according to the information which they severally have given to me.
Touching further upon this unemployment problem it seems to me that the two most important aspects of it, if you can single two out from many, are those of the soldier veteran and the youth of the country. As to the former I understand a special opportunity will arise later when we come to consider a report; therefore I need say nothing about it at the present time. But, sir, it is impossible to overstate the importance of youth training and youth reclamation work. If the government of the day had done nothing else, its advance upon this problem during the recess would be sufficient to entitle it to the continued confidence of the people. What has been done is not so much in itself as an earnest of what is to be. Now, according to the speech from the throne the work is to be continued and the plan enlarged.
I have kept in very close touch with youth, both employed and unemployed, and I believe there is no sadder sight, and one could not have a sadder experience, than to find young men and young women hopeless because jobless. We seem always to be in danger of falling into the needless use of superlatives in discussing problems of this sort; yet even at that risk I say that I do not believe any country has any other assets quite equal in value to its youth. Continuing the thought of the youth of our country being wealth, I think I am justified in saying that youth is the greatest jewel of the country. And to permit idleness among youth, to such an extent at any rate as to sap their morale or begin to render them incapable of seizing

The Address-Mr. Walsh
opportunities when they arise, is comparable with throwing your jewels into the sea. No price is too great to pay to prevent this from happening, and no price that can be paid hereafter will restore our loss if we permit it to happen.
Now, as I have already indicated, there is much that I should like to see done. I have expressed dissatisfaction with some things; I have failed to express the satisfaction that I feel with many other things, but time does not permit. While I have various aspirations and aims and ideals I would sacrifice them all and accept anything if I knew that the young people of the country were being saved for the country; that they were going to get their chance. As far as I am concerned everything else may go by the board if youth gets its chance. And observing what has been done and realizing that more is now to be done in the way of training and reclamation of youth, I feel that in this respect at any rate I should be content. There is more hope in that one section of the speech from the throne than in any other part of it.

There is no doubt in my mind that the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne have been amply congratulated by hon. members of the house. I would not wish to make the expression commonplace by repeating it; nevertheless my feelings are just as sincere towards those two gentlemen as the feelings of those who have already expressed them in more graceful language. I know that the task committed to the charge of those two newly elected members was a delicate one, and involved a rather heavy responsibility. The government could have made their task more pleasant, more enjoyable and more satisfactory if they had brought before the house something of a more commendable nature by way of an address. Very unfortunately the newly elected members had rather a bare bone on which to chew. It was unfortunate for them that they had to make their initial speeches under such circumstances; nevertheless even under those circumstances they acquitted themselves well, and I add my congratulations to those already extended.
I should like also to pay my tribute, humble but sincere, to the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) on an honour that has come to him in recent months. It is an honour well deserved, and I am sure that there is not a member of the house, on either side, who is not sincere in expressing his congratulations to the right hon. gentleman. I hope he has a long life still ahead of him
in which he may enjoy the full vigour of health, so that in due course we on this side will have the privilege of addressing him, sitting to the left of the Speaker, as the right hon. former Minister of Justice.
May I express the hope that the mover of the address has left behind him a certain atmosphere which must have accumulated during his long term of service in the legislature of Quebec, and particularly during the last few years of that service, when he had the misfortune to be a member of the now famous Taschereau regime. I am hoping that in the pleasant surroundings of this house, with the congenial companionship that he will find here on both sides, he will soon learn that he has migrated to a vastly different atmosphere, and that anything he has said or done in the past will be completely forgotten. I followed the campaign in Lotbiniere with some degree of interest, for it has been my privilege to know the newly elected member for that constituency for a number of years. I remember him in Quebec in 1917, during rather troublesome times, rather hectic days in that province, when the lives of certain politicians of a certain faith were not worth a great deal. I remember him. as a member of the legislative assembly, rising in his seat and moving a resolution which I desire to read. I am sure hon. members will appreciate this reference, which will enable them better to understand the antecedents from which the hon. member has graduated. At that time the hon. gentleman was a member of the Quebec legislature for the constituency of Lotbiniere, the same constituency which he now represents in this house. This is the resolution he moved;
This house is of opinion that the province of Quebec will be disposed to accept rupture of the federal pact of 1867 if in the opinion of the other provinces it is believed that the said province is an obstacle to the union, to the progress and the development of Canada.
Unfortunately they do not keep a record of the proceedings in that legislature such as we have here. Otherwise I should have had an opportunity of reading some of .the choice phrases then used by the hon. gentleman in support of this resolution. That, however, indicates the atmosphere which the hon. gentleman has left, and I wish him well in the atmosphere he is now enjoying.
I should like also to direct the attention of the house to the misuse of the result of that by-election in Lotbiniere. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) characterized it, in his usual manner, as another evidence that the people of this country were well satisfied with the policies of the present government. You will excuse me, Mr. Speaker,

The Address-Mr. Walsh
for using the word "policies"; I use it because the Prime Minister also used it. For my part I fail to see any policy that the present government has, but those were the terms the Prime Minister saw fit to use. I want to point out that the policies of the present government were not discussed during the by-election in Lotbiniere. I should like to quote a statement by the present member for Lotbiniere. who was the candidate representing the Liberal party in that by-election. This statement appeared in L'Action Catho-lique, which is published in the city of Quebec, and which certainly is not a Conservative paper:
The victorious candidate expressed himself as "flatly opposed to our spending one single dollar, one single cent, to equip and send one sole soldier to a war foreign to Canada."
I compared that with the statement made in Paris by the Prime Minister, and I could not, understand how the right hon. gentleman could suggest that the success of his candidate in Lotbiniere indicated the goodwill of the people towards the policies of the present government. This is the statement made by the Prime Minister, and I contrast it with the statement made from a public platform by the present member for Lotbiniere:
Some people have been implying since the imperial conference that Canada wished to withdraw more from the affairs of the commonwealth of British nations. This is entirely untrue. We like to manage our own affairs, but any threat to England would immediately bring Canada to her side.
That is a quotation from the London Times. It is, I should say, rather opposed to the statement by the hon. member for Lotbiniere.
I should like to emphasize the point I am making, namely that the election of the hon. member for Lotbiniere was no vindication of the policy of the present government, by quoting again from L'Action Catholique:
It appears that in certain circles the great victory of the Hon. J. N. Francceur in Lotbiniere is interpreted as an approbation of a policy of armament.
There should not be a mistaken idea on this point. Inasmuch as the electorate of Lotbiniere endorsed the present armament policy it was with the condition that these armaments serve exclusively for the defence of Canada. To pretend that Lotbiniere expressed its willingness to give a blank cheque for armaments would be going pretty far.
If Mr. Francoeur and Mr. Lapointe had showed themselves less hostile to participation in imperialistic wars, the result would have been quite different, even in a county that is Liberal by tradition. . . . The vote in Lotbiniere is a frankly anti-imperialist vote.
I want the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) to note that state-

ment, because he was given to making certain misstatements in the by-election in Victoria which would lead the people in that section of the country to believe that the present government was very much pro-imperialistic.
While we are on the subject of by-elections may I for a moment digress to speak about the by-election in Victoria. I feel that the manner in which that by-election was conducted, from the Liberal side, was a disgrace to the public life of Canada. I consider that if there is any justification for the formation of fascist and communist organizations in Canada, they will find a certain justification in the statements made from public platforms by men who are presumed to be enjoying public confidence and to hold responsible positions. The people are losing confidence in those men in high office. They are losing confidence because of the rash, ridiculous statements these people make to win by-elections.
May I draw to the attention of the house a statement made by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) in support of the expenditure of certain moneys at the Pacific coast for armament and defence I quote from the Victoria Daily Times of November 19, a paper which is probably more pro-Liberal than any other paper in Canada:
The minister referred to the appropriation for this purpose, for British Columbia increased from the 1935-36 total of the Bennett regime of $1,916,000 to $5,817,000 with an additional $2,346,000 for air equipment. This was a program for the Pacific coast from Prince Rupert to Esquimalt, including points at Vancouver and Vancouver Island which could not be completed until 1940.
"If I am here," said the minister, "not as a Liberal or as a politician but as Minister of National Defence, who has had some difficulty in this program to ask you to indicate to the government do you approve of these policies of security for the Pacific coast, or do you not?"
Mr. Mackenzie mentioned he had had some difficulty in securing these estimates and urged Victoria electors to give their endorsement by sending to Ottawa a man who could assist him.
Mr. Mackenzie pointed out the naval magazine in Esquimalt had been condemned as far back as 1905 but nothing had been done about it until the Liberal government did it, and told how Canada's forces had been starved to deterioration during the depression.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and members of the house, this question: Does any man with a high sense of public responsibility feel that under the circumstances those statements by the Minister of National Defence were justified? I ask hon. members to consider those statements carefully. We voted to his department the sum of $35,000,000 to be used for purposes of national defence. That was to be administered as a sacred trust fund by the Minister of National Defence, through

The Address-Mr. Walsh
the department over which he has control. But instead of administering it as a sacred trust he saw fit to bring it on to the political platform, to parade it before the electorate of Victoria and to state to them, " In view of the fact that through my department I have spent $5,000,000 or $6,000,000, therefore you should support the Liberal candidate." Appeals of that nature are most degrading, and are not in any way uplifting in the minds of our people. Sooner or later such appeals are going to undermine the democratic principles we enjoy. I make that statement without animosity, feeling that I am speaking in the public interest. I say it because I feel that every man and woman in Canada with any understanding of the responsibility of that minister feels that he no longer is justified in holding his present position and in asking for a further appropriation of about $30,000,000 to be spent in a similar manner during the coming year.
I would develop the point at greater length, but I notice the time is slipping by. I had intended, however, to refer to the statements made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, when in the course of the by-election he took advantage of a last minute broadcast, so that no reply could be given. In that broadcast he made statements which were justified neither by fact nor even by possibility of fact. In putting before the public certain information which he must have known would not bear close scrutiny, and which he knew would not receive close scrutiny, on account of the fact the contest was almost at an end, I believe he transgressed even the ordinary rules of debate. In one part of his observations he said this:
The real issue in Victoria's by-election that has been made by Mr. Bennett is: "Are you in Victoria going to support the government of Canada going along with Great Britain and other nations of the empire in working out a world trade policy, suitable to the needs of 1937, or are you going to stay with Mr. Bennett on his ' Canada First ' program of 1930," said Mr. McGeer. " Are you going to vote for the empire and empire unity, or are you going to vote for Mr. Bennett's condemnation of the empire policy developed at the imperial conference in 1937."
I have not seen tabled in the house any report of an imperial trade agreement or an imperial policy embodying a trade agreement, as a result of the imperial conference of 1937, and neither has the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard. The policy he was enunciating there is a direct development of that policy enunciated in 1930 by the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and the direct result of the empire trade agreements reached in this building in 1932. Yet in a last minute broadcast the hon. member 51952-18
for Vancouver-Burrard would wish the people of Victoria to understand that those trade agreements were the result of the imperial conference of 1937, and that the present government should take credit for development along those lines.
The hon. member went even farther, and made a comparison of figures. Of course he was most happy in his choice of figures. It was his desire to suggest that the trade agreement with the United States had shown a very favourable trade balance in favour of Canada. In giving the figures he stopped where it was convenient for him to stop, namely, at the end of August. He failed to go on to give the figures for September, October and November. If I may be permitted to do so I shall now set them out. For September, October and November of 1936 we had a favourable Canadian balance of $25,366,000. That is the figure arrived at after comparing the imports of Canada from the United States with the exports of Canada to the United States. For the same three months of 1937, however, we find a favourable United States trade balance of $19,597,000. Hon. members will recall that when we were discussing the agreement the leader of the opposition and his colleagues suggested that the market in the United States was a most uncertain one, and that we in Canada should be dependent upon the more certain market offered in Great Britain. This is proven by the figures. The trade balance is now against us and in favour of the United States and is likely to continue so.
Just one more reference to the Victoria byelection. The premier of British Columbia gave vigorous support to the Liberal candidate, and assured his audiences during the campaign that they need fear no contamination from a Liberal candidate being elected for Victoria. He expressed the feeling that the government would see that the beneficial results of the British Empire agreements were consolidated and retained so far as Canada was concerned. On more than one occasion he assured his audiences that such would be the case. After assuring them during the course of the by-election that that would be the case, why did he do a loop-the-loop act in the provincial legislature in order to bolster up his own position in the province? After assuring audiences in Victoria that they had nothing to fear from the present government so far as empire trade agreements were concerned, listen to this motion which was moved

The Address-Mr. Walsh

early in December by the premier of British Columbia himself and forwarded to the government at Ottawa:
This house favours the principle of empire prt ferenees and urges upon the dominion government the great importance to British Columbia of the maintenance of existing markets in Great Britain and other parts of the empire.
After deceiving the people of Victoria, telling them they had nothing to fear, he brings forward this resolution in the legislature at Victoria requesting the present government at Ottawa to safeguard what the previous Conservative government had won in 1932.
I was going to refer to the St. Henry by-election, but that has already been referred to. Lavish promises were made in that campaign by ministers who are at present members of this house. I want to read a statement made by the member-elect, now the member for St. Henry (Mr. Bonnier) shortly after his election. It shows a very high standard of public idealism. The member-elect was interviewed, and this is the substance of the interview. He was asked if he was going to retain a double mandate, namely, the honour of being alderman for St. Paul ward in the city of Montreal as well as being member of parliament for St. Henry, and he assured them that such was his intention:
" Why not," answered the councilman for St. Paul ward. "The people in my district have given me their confidence. I am ready to fulfil a double mandate and remain on Parliament Hill as well as at the city hall-"
I want the house to notice what follows:
"-to get public works which had been promised for my division."
What high idealism! He comes here to help solve our national problems, and here we have his reason for being in this house supporting the present government-to get public works for his division. What public works? The interview continues:
First, a tunnel under the Lachine canal. Then the abolition of railway tracks and level crossings in St. Henry. This would come with the construction of the Canadian National Railway station at the site of the big hole on Dorchester street. I also figure on getting a bridge to link the down-under division with the Notre Dame de Grace area. After his federal division gets these, he'll say good-bye to Ottawa. Concordia is enough for him.
We welcome, Mr. Speaker, to this house the hon. member for St. Henry, who will be of considerable assistance to both sides in bringing to bear important opinion upon our great national questions. Does the house realize that what has been promised in St. Henry involves the expenditure at the very

least of $50,000,000? Is one by-election in St. Henry worth the price of $50,000,000? And, remember, the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) said that this would be done before the next election. It is not worth it, and it lowers the standard by which public life is viewed by the public of Canada when we have statements of that kind from our public men, seeking to come here to help solve our great national problems.
I was going on to relate other incidents, but I shall close that part of my remarks.
I was going to refer to the Taschereau government in Quebec that is now out of office. Many of the supporters of that government are now supporting this government. I assume they are glad to get away from the kind of atmosphere which prevailed down there. They have a better atmosphere in that province now. The only comparison I was able to find in Canadian history with the Taschereau government, defeated in the province of Quebec in 1936, was the famous "Hug-the-machine" Liberal government in the province of Ontario. Every time I look at Canadian history from the point of view of standards of public life it seems that it is generally, if not always, a Liberal government which is involved in conditions of the kind to which I have made passing reference.
How about the Roblin government?

For every Conservative gov- [DOT] eminent that can be named, I can name two or three Liberal governments that fell, and fell far more badly, from grace than any Conservative government ever knew how to fall. That brings to my mind a conversation which took place on the train between Montreal and Ottawa. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) will remember a very pleasant trip we had in the fall. I was talking to a gentleman on the train coming here to do business, or at least he thought he was going to do business, with the Department of National Defence, and he wanted to know where the department was. "Do you know," he said, "what I am going up for? For thirteen years my firm has had regular business from the department, and now I have not heard from them for over a year." I said, "There must be some mistake. You will find them pretty nice fellows over there." I came back on the train with him and asked him how he had got along. "Not so good," he said. "What happened?" I asked. He told me he had asked them why he had not received any inquiries or any orders, and he said they told him, "Well, you do not manufacture your

The Address-Mr. Walsh
goods in Canada." "Oh, yes," he said, "we do. We have a big plant in Montreal, and all our material, containers and everything else, is made in Montreal." Well, that did not go over so good. They said to him. "Your name is not on the list." "What list?" he asked. They said, "The patronage list." "Oh," he said, "I did not know there was any such list." "Oh, yes, there is," they told him. "Then by what means do I get my name on that list?" he asked. "I am afraid you will have to see the patronage committee in Montreal," they said.
Now that is a fact, Mr. Speaker, and that is what I understand is regularly taking place in a great many departments of the government at Ottawa. There, at any rate, is one illustration that I know is an absolute fact.
I was going to speak of the attitude of the present government towards provincial legislation. I was going to ask why they had not done something about the Ontario legislation and the so-called padlock legislation referring to communists in the province of Quebec, but I see my time will not permit. In passing let me say that I do not agree with the padlock law. I agree with the object which the premier of Quebec has in view, but I do not agree with the method he is pursuing by putting that statute on the books. I want to say in justification of the premier of that province that he is no separatist. He is not trying to bring about disunion in Canada. Listen to these words of Premier Duplessis, spoken at Longueuil on January 15:
No separatist spirit can prevail in the province of Quebec, for the province intends to remain an integral part of the dominion.
That is his attitude, and that attitude he will maintain. Although we find him opposed to changes in the British North America Act, there are good and sufficient reasons, for he belongs, so far as the dominion is concerned, to a minority race. In that province I myself belong to a minority race, and I am in agreement with him and with my friend the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) that there should be no changes in the British North America Act but that we should endeavour to meet conditions as they arise by some other method than that proposed by the present government.
I was also going to refer, if time would allow, to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, but that matter has already been amply covered. I only wish to say that I am in entire disagreement with the policy which is being pursued by this government. Naturally I disagree with the increase in the licence fee from two dollars to two and a half dollars, 51952-184
but that is of minor importance. I disagree with the principle of their policy. You cannot have growing up in this country a publicly owned institution along with a privately owned institution of the same nature. Either you have to adopt the British broadcasting system or the system in the United States. The institution should be either publicly owned or privately owned. It cannot be jockeyed midway between the two. It is not fair to the privately owned stations or to the ratepayers of this country to put the corporation in competition with regular business. As hon. members know, one of the principles of government is that the government should not engage in business but should strive to regulate business. I believe the radio is of national and international importance, and for that reason it should be put on the same basis as the post office, on the same basis as the telegraph and telephone systems of Great Britain, and made a public utility supported by the government for the convenience of the people living within the dominion.
I also intended to refer to the Americanization of our purchasers in this country, but that has already been satisfactorily covered.
As regards the railway situation, I can refer to it because in the speech from the throne it is covered by a negligible quantity of words, in fact no words at all. There is no reference to what the government proposes to do to solve this great problem. It is on our hands. It is not of Conservative creation. I do not intend to review the history of this problem; it is sufficient to say that it is of such magnitude as to require immediate attention. Liberal members when they were sitting on this side of the house urged the then Conservative government to deal courageously with this matter. Have the Liberals dealt courageously with it? What have they done since coming into office towards solving the railway problem? They have done two things. First, against the express recommendation of the Duff commission they did away with the trustee system and established a board of directors. Second, they introduced last year Bill No. 12, to create a new financial set-up for the new Canadian National Railways, thereby taking away from the railway's statement that which meant anything to the citizens of Canada, in that it showed them exactly what that system meant financially to this country. I have in my hand a resolution which was passed by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, at Vancouver, requesting the government to take "resolute and constructive action to solve the railway
The Address-Mr. Walsh

problem." I have another resolution from the Federation des Chambres de Commerce de la province de Quebec. After reciting their reasons for making the resolution for presentation to the government, it continues:
Be it resolved, that representations be made to the government of Canada urging the pressing necessity of adopting effective measures to secure the most economical operation of Canada's railway systems, in order not only to eliminate the deficits of the Canadian National railways, thereby reducing the drain on the federal treasury, but also to improve the financial position of the privately-owned railway whose good credit means so much to Canada as a whole.
These organizations represent a large body of public opinion. Yet the present government are giving no lead in the direction of a possible solution of this gigantic problem. I trust that during the course of this session we on this 3ide of the house will be given ample opportunity to discuss the possibilities of a solution. Mr. C. H. Carlisle, president of the Dominion Bank, says that the country's great railway problem would be the more speedily and efficiently settled were it free from party politics. I quite agree. I suggest that it can be settled by the present parliament. In this house are hon. members who are conversant with that problem, public spirited citizens representing all parties, and if a special committee of the house were appointed and the government bound themselves to accept a unanimous report from that committee, I believe that in sitting around a table and forgetting our politics we would soon reach an agreement and a settlement that would be advantageous alike to Canada, to the Canadian National Railways, and to the privately owned corporation, the Canadian Pacific railway. I am not advocating unification, but I do believe it is the only solution so far presented which merits some consideration. I am prepared to receive other suggestions and give them equal consideration, but I honestly believe that a select committee of the house could settle this problem during the course of the present session and relieve Canada of the financial milestone which hangs around her neck. Do hon. members realize that, of the total debt of the dominion, namely $4,750,000,000, over fifty per cent is directly chargeable to the Canadian National Railways and to our venture into public ownership? When hon. members are confronted with facts of that nature they will readily understand why I feel, as others do, that it is urgent that the present government and the present parliament should tackle the problem involved in

our railways in the courageous manner suggested by an hon. member, a Liberal member, when he was sitting on this side of the house.
One last word. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has placed before parliament the main estimates for the coming year. They amount to $418,968,899, and compare with estimates last year of $410,465,397, representing an increase of $8,503,502. The supplementary estimates are still to come. Is it not unfortunate that, knowing that the people of Canada are overburdened with taxation, the present government cannot see its way clear to reduce rather than to increase expenditure? To that total of $8,503,000 I want to add this figure: During the year there was saved by the present government through a policy of conversion the sum of $6,000,000. That has also been spent, so that the total increase this year over the same estimates of last year is $14,503,502, a tremendous increase, a stupendous amount of money for the parliament of Canada to be spending on a population of eleven million. I leave it to hon. members to figure out the per capita of that expenditure; I leave it to them to say whether such an increase is at all justifiable;
I leave it to them to say whether they are playing fair with the people of Canada in increasing rather than reducing government expenditure.
The present government came into office on promises to reduce expenditures, to reduce taxation. Have we seen any material evidence of action in that direction? The first step this government took was to increase the revenue by increasing the sales tax from six to eight per cent Their next step now is to add a further burden of fifty cents a set on radios and to extend the fee to all sets which anyone may have within the precincts of his home. What other steps are going to be taken by the government to increase taxation still further it is hard to say, and probably only one with a vivid imagination can guess what expenditures will be required by them before they leave office.
Is there anything of political significance in the increase in the amount of money required by the present government as shown by the estimates? Do they contemplate an election? Do they contemplate fulfilling some of the rash promises they made in Victoria, St. Henry, and other parts of the country? I would ask the hon member for St. Henry to go through the estimates carefully. If he does so he will not find in them any reference to a tunnel under the Lachine canal; he will not find any reference to the removal of railway tracks from his division of St. Henry;

The Address-Mr. Tucker
he will not find any reference to an appropriation to be used to fill the hole on Dorchester street; nor will he find anything that will lead him to believe that the present government is going to build a bridge from the lower St. Henry division to the section of Notre Dame de Grace.
I leave these thoughts with hon. members and with the government, and ask them to look at the facts from a non-partisan point of view, so far as expenditures, radio and railways are concerned, and to give the public for once in their lives a really square deal.

My first words in this third session of the present parliament will be those of congratulation to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the way he represented our country at the coronation of the king and queen last summer. I am sure the whole of Canada was delighted with our representation at that time. My next words will be those of congratulation to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) on the honour conferred upon him in being made a member of the British privy council. Regardless of race or creed, Canadians of all classes from one end of the country to the other, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, regard the right hon. the Minister of Justice as a great Canadian. My next words will be those of congratulation to the mover (Mr. Francoeur) and the seconder (Mr. Warren) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It would be presumptuous on my part to emphasize that because they are both older parliamentarians than myself. I can only express the hope that they will both be long spared to serve the country in this house.
I do not intend to follow the last speaker (Mr. Walsh), but there are one or two remarks which I think I should make in reference to his speech. He suggests that in some way Liberals are inclined to be more corrupt than Conservatives; in fact, he seems to think the Conservatives are so virtuous that they can afford to point the finger at us. I suggest to the hon. gentleman that the people of Canada are tired of mud-slinging between parties; what they want to know is what we are going to do to solve some of their problems. Furthermore, we do not need any lessons in virtue or political honesty from the Tory party.
May I express the appreciation of the people of Saskatchewan of the aid given them in the greatest calamity that has ever befallen any province in the history of Canada. First of all, we appreciate the voluntary aid so
generously extended by all parts of the country, especially by the farming population, many of whom were not in any too good shape themselves. We realize that now more than ever, since hearing the speech of the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman). In order to help us, many of these people filled cars with the produce of their own labour, which produce they could ill afford to give away. It showed a magnificent spirit of Canadian fellowship. Let me also, on behalf of Saskatchewan, exprpss appreciation of the generous aid given by the government of Canada. It was no more generous than the situation demanded; nevertheless we were glad to know that in our troubles the rest of Canada had no objection to the government coming to our aid. I wish to say how much western Canada appreciates also the energy of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who went there and covered the ground by automobile, making a thorough study of the situation. I believe, as most of the people of Saskatchewan believe, that on the whole he dealt effectively and satisfactorily with the greatest problem which any minister of the crown will probably have to face during the time this government may be in office. The task needs only to be seen to be appreciated. It is the greatest problem that has ever faced any government in connection with drought in our history.
Let me now pass on to some remarks that have been made arising out of that help, which we think had a great deal to do with demonstrating the essential unity of confederation, and the fact that we are consciously a nation. Incidentally, before I forget, there is one thing more I would say to the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. He seemed to suggest that the people of Quebec, the people of Lotbiniere, were unique in being inveterately opposed to purely imperialistic wars. My father was born in Ontario of British stock; I was born in Manitoba, and I do not think anyone in Quebec is more opposed to imperialistic wars than I and those like me of British stock, the young people of Canada, from one end of the country to the other. Does the hon. gentleman suggest that he is favourable to war as a part of imperialism? If he does, he should belong to another age. Wars of imperialistic conquest in democratic countries should be a thing of the past, especially since we have seen something of the horrors, the miseries, the frustrations and the unutterable unhappiness caused by war-and I have seen a little of it all myself. In the
The Address-Mr. Tucker

face of all this, no one in this house should condemn anyone for saying that he is opposed to imperialistic wars.
Would the hon. member permit me to say that I am in hearty agreement with what he has just said.

I am glad to hear it, Mr. Speaker. The verdict in Lotbiniere should not be regarded as an endorsation of imperialistic wars. I do not think anyone ever thought it could be so regarded.
The suggestion has been made by some people in the central part of Canada-I am glad to say I do not think they are in the majority; in fact I hope they are only a very small group-that the west is becoming too great a burden and that it would be a good thing for the east if they could get rid of the burden of the west. To us in the west that suggestion came as a great shock. We in western Canada have felt that we have suffered more than any other part of Canada through the tariffs and fiscal policies adopted by Canadian governments. The attitude of western Canada has been that the people of those plains were being exploited as no British people had ever been exploited before; but in spite of this, they never suggested that they wanted to break away from Canada or cease to be part of the Canadian nation. Now in the time of our need, to be told by some people in eastern Canada that they would like to secede from us, after the patience that we feel we have shown with the rest of Canada, comes to us as a great shock. In that connection I should like to read some words from the foreword written by Premier Patterson of Saskatchewan to the brief presented to the Rowell commission, which I think indicate the attitude of the people of Saskatchewan towards Canada and towards the disabilities under which we suffer. He said:
We realize that confederation was established for the good of all Canada and that each province must be prepared to make its contribution to the common good. . . . We believe it essential that a united Canada should be maintained as a part of the British Commonwealth of Nations, and are prepared to devote every effort to that end.
That, I think, is the attitude of ninety-nine per cent of the people who inhabit western Canada. They believe in Canada as their country. But they say to their fellow Canadians from one end of Canada to the other, We expect to be treated as well as are the people in any other part of Canada. If, fot example, we can show in connection with

our educational system that we have not the money to bring up our young people properly and educate them as good Canadians, we expect you will do enough to enable us to maintain at least a minimum standard of Canadian citizenship; in other words, that you will not drive us down to a peasant level. That is the attitude the people of western Canada take, that all that is necessary is to lay the facts before the people of Canada, as is being done in connection with the Rowell commission, and then we have only to sit back and confidently expect that the people of Canada will do us justice. That is one of the reasons I intend to vote for the motion and against the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). This government has given western Canada a chance to lay its grievances before a tribunal which will make a finding on those grievances, and thus some hope is held out that some of the disabilities under which we have suffered for many years will receive attention and redress.
I intended to go into some figures indicating how important western Canada is to the rest of the country, but I do not think I should do that here because I am sure that everyone in Canada, from the lumbering industry on the Pacific coast to the manufacturing industries of eastern Canada, realizes that the building-up of western Canada and the production of immense wealth there made a great contribution to the upbuilding of Canada as a whole. I might give one figure. The value of grain production in the prairie provinces in the twenty-seven years from 1910 to 1936 inclusive was $10,278,465,000. That in very large measure went to increase the wealth of the central part of Canada-goodness knows we do not have it now in western Canada.
A charge often brought against the people of western Canada is that their governments have been extravagant and that is why we are in our present difficulties. In answer to that let me say that so far as Saskatchewan is concerned, in 1929 when the government led by the present Minister of Agriculture went out of office the debt in Saskatchewan was only slightly over $63,000,000. It was one of the lowest per capita debts in the whole of Canada; I think only Quebec and Prince Edward Island had a lower per capita debt at that time than Saskatchewan. Since then we have had to spend vast sums on relief, to advance moneys that the banks had to pay in respect of pool guarantees, and other things arising out of drought and low prices for our products

The Address-Mr. Tucker
which have increased our debt to almost $200,000,000 to-day. But I ask hon. members to remember that we provided our legislative buildings and everything we had in the way of capital equipment prior to 1929 with a debt of only $63,000,000, every cent of which was represented by actual physical assets in the way of public buildings, roads, bridges and so on. That hardly bears out the charge of extravagance. What has happened since has been no fault of ours.
Then we hear the charge that the people of the west are extravagant. Every farmer has a carl Well, some figures have been given here as to the kind of houses that most of the farming people in the west have to live in; I do not intend to deal with that. But I wish to give some figures bearing on this matter, and I hope I shall be pardoned if I take Ontario for comparison, because I do not wish to burden the house with too many figures. Comparing farmers in each case, I find that in Ontario the proportion of farmers having motor cars is 65-4 per cent. What about the extravagant farmers of Saskatchewan? Only 47-7 per cent of Saskatchewan farmers had motor cars. That was in 1931; since then of course the proportion of Saskatchewan farmers having motor cars will be very much less.
Then in regard to telephones, in Saskatchewan the proportion having telephones is 34-2 per cent, while in Ontario it is 54-1 per cent. If there is a place where telephones are needed it certainly is Saskatchewan. Just yesterday I received a letter from a doctor friend of mine in Rosthern. informing me that in a village about fourteen miles distant there was a woman very sick. Last year the municipality had a municipal doctor not very far away, but on account of their financial difficulty they could not keep him. In the middle of the night in forty below zero weather this doctor was called to attend that woman. They had trouble on the way with their snowmobile, and by the time the doctor got there the woman was dead. Such things are not uncommon occurrences in Saskatchewan where doctors live too far away to be obtained quickly. When we see our people forced through poverty to endure such things, is it any wonder that we come here and ask that you give us all the consideration you feel we deserve as Canadian citizens? Certainly we need telephones in Saskatchewan, but in 1931 only 34-2 per cent of the people had them.
Only 20-2 per cent of the farmers in Saskatchewan have radios; in Ontario the percentage is 21-5. Gas and electric light in the home- 16'8 per cent in Ontario and only 2-8 per cent in Saskatchewan; piped water in the
kitchen-10-4 per cent in Ontario and only 1-4 per cent in Saskatchewan. What, then, about this charge of extravagant westerners?
