As a matter of fact I was born and brought up in the west, and from what I know of the way our people live out there I say they live just as close to a minimum standard of living as any people in the whole of Canada.
I hope no one will object to my giving my next figures, but in doing so I have in mind some remarks made by some public men in Ontario. Take the figures in regard to the sale of liquor. In Saskatchewan in 1929, receipts from the sale of beer were $4,262,000. By 1934 they had decreased by about two-thirds, or to about $1,422,000. Receipts from the sale of hard liquor had decreased from $3,339,000 in 1929 to $S40,000 in 1934. What has been the history in Ontario? In the year ended March 31, 1937, in Ontario I understand some $72,000,000 was spent on intoxicants. The gallonage of spirits increased by 71 per cent; of wine by 31 per cent and of beer by 211 per cent in a period of two years. In saying that I am not finding fault with the people of Ontario. If they want and can afford to enjoy their beer they are lucky; but I ask them, when finding fault with the extravagance of the people of western Canada, to remember that while they were drinking many times more beer than they were two years ago, our people were drinking just one-third as much.
What has brought about the position in which western Canada finds itself, if its people have worked hard and have not been extravagant either individually or in their government? Well, I wish to indicate in outline some of the reasons why we find ourselves in our present position.
In the first place we are in the centre of the continent. Practically everything we sell must be sold on the markets of the world. The price we get in those markets is brought back to us less the amount necessary to send those goods to market. Take wheat, for example. The average cost of sending wheat from Saskatchewan to the world market is about 35 cents a bushel. We get what is paid in the markets of the world, less 35 cents. On almost everything we buy we must pay the freight to bring it to us. For example, a person buying a cheap car in Ontario pays $124 less in freight on that car than we pay in Saskatchewan. In other words, we are caught in regard to freight in both shipping out and bringing things in.
If anyone is interested in this question of freight, a study of the Saskatchewan brief presented to the Rowell commission will indicate that in western Canada freight is charged
The Address-Mr. Tucker

on a higher basis than in eastern Canada. In other words, freight seems to be based upon what the traffic will bear. In Ontario, with water transportation competing, the railroads have had to keep freight rates down. Our only protection has been the Crowsnest pass rates and if you study rates you will find that western Canada is paying more for freight than is being paid in eastern Canada, over equal distances.
Another thing that has injured western Canada is of course the tariff policy. Something has been said about the figures given by the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) before a commission investigating the matter in Nova Scotia. There is no question, I believe, in the mind of any thinking man but that the tariff must operate against the primary producer in western Canada. The price of everything he sells is fixed in the markets of the world, where he is competing with agriculturists all over the world. I do not care how low their standard of living may be, the western Canadian farmer has to compete with them. Then he is forced to buy the things he has to purchase in one of the most expensive markets in the world. That may have been all right, Mr. Speaker, when there was a vast amount of new land available which cost the farmer very little, but the time has come when the fact must be faced that the western Canadian farmer cannot bear that burden any longer. It may be all right to say that we need this protection in order to make sure that large profits can be made in our textile industiy; in order that our automobile industry may have large profits; in order that we may pay large salaries to the executives of automobile concerns, and so on. If we could afford that luxury it would not be so important, but the time has come when the house must choose between not driving the western farmer out of existence and those other things I have mentioned. It is no longer a matter of argument; the western Canadian farmer has reached a point where, if you do not give him relief by way of reduction of tariffs he cannot carry on.
That is the question which must be faced by the house. Any study of the present position of the western Canadian farmer must lead anyone to that conclusion. Consider, for example, the load of debt. We had last year $525,000,000 approximately of private debt alone in Saskatchewan. There has been a reduction of that debt. That reduction in regard to mortgages and agreements has amounted to $26,000,000; in regard to taxes, $22,000,000 and in regard to relief write-offs, $31,000,000, or a total of $79,000,000. Then

there was a reduction in 1937 under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act amounting to another $3,000,000. Under private arrangement there was a reduction of about $1,000,000, and last year there were payments of taxes, debts and so on amounting to about $12,500,000. That means that we can deduct about S95,500,000 from that amount of $525,000,000. But last year we had interest on agreements for sale, mortgages and other debts amounting to at least $25,000,000; municipal tax levies totalling another $12,500,000 and relief advances of $15,000,000, bringing the debt, in spite of all that has been done by way of debt reduction, back to about $482,000,000, or $15 per acre on all the crop land To have paid interest alone on this debt would have taken nearly two-thirds of the cash receipts from wheat available for sale in almost every year since 1930, and municipal taxes would have taken the rest.
Can anyone tell me, then, that we can carry on if we must bear one cent more of burden than we should be carrying? If we are to compete in the markets of the world our only hope is to say to the Canadian farmer, "You have a load on your back. You must compete with some of the lowest paid agricultural workers in the world, and the only way you can do so is by being enabled to buy the things you need in the very cheapest market." That is the situation, whether we like it or not, and if you do not want all the western Canadian farmers being forced to come east to try to get on relief in your cities you will deal with that problem.
As a matter of fact, what has happened in that very connection? Our natural increase, that is, the excess of births over deaths, in Saskatchewan from 1931 to 1936 was 70,000. Immigration to Saskatchewan during that period amounted to 3.500. What is the actual situation to-day? What do we find, after having had an excess of 70,000 births over deaths and 3,500 people coming into the province? There are less males in the province to-day than there were in 1931. We find that the actual increase, including males and females, was only 9,108. In other words, we find that largely of her native born sons and daughters Saskatchewan lost over 64,000. I ask people from the maritimes, Ontario or Quebec if it is a proper condition when we find that 64,000 of our best young citizens are driven out to seek their living elsewhere. That is what is happening in Saskatchewan.
Let us now consider the value of farm property. In 1921 tlhe value of the average farm, with equipment, was $13,814, while in 1936 that value had shrunk to $7,185. The number of farms owned by those farming

The Address-Mr. Tucker
them provides an interesting comparison. In 1911, 91 per cent of the farms in Saskatchewan were owned by those farming them.; in 1921 the percentage had dropped to 80-5 per cent: in 1931, to 70-5 per cent, and in 1936. to 65-2 per cent,-and so it goes on. How long are we going to sit idly by and permit that condition to prevail?
Before leaving the question of debt reduction may I say that the present board of review operating in Saskatchewan has brought a measure of relief very much appreciated and very necessary to the people of our province. But it cannot keep up with the work coming in. I suggest that in order that it may perform that work at least one more board of review should be set up to deal with the accumulation of cases, and that it should act under the direction of the present chairman of the board. I know that people in other parts of Canada have found fault with the act. I would suggest that if people in Ontario or Quebec find the act is not working out satisfactorily in those provinces an amendment might be made whereby any province might exempt itself from its operation. Provision might be made in an amendment to the act whereby any provincial legislature might pass a resolution to the effect that that province need not remain under the act, and that thereafter it stand repealed in that particular province. I have no doubt as to the constitutionality of such a move, because in connection with the criminal code we find that different parts apply differently in different sections of the dominion. So long as we have jurisdiction to deal with the matter I submit there could be no doubt that we could make it apply in one province, and not in another
It came into force by proclamation in every province.

Yes, it came into force
by proclamation in every province. As a matter of fact I believe there is provision in the act whereby, unless she desires, the act shall not apply to British Columbia.
And all the provinces are in the same position.

May I place before hon. members the history of interest in Saskatchewan. In that province we had mortgages bearing as high as ten per cent interest. Although it is provided in the Bank Act that banks shall not charge more than seven per cent we had banks closing their eyes to that provision and charging as high as nine per cent. I believe I noticed in the headlines of the papers as I was entering the building to-night that the banks have this year made
half a million dollars in increased profits. I suggest that it be ascertained how much the banks have taken in interest from the people in western Canada, over and above the amount of seven per cent to which they were entitled, and that that amount be set aside to provide university scholarships for the children of the people they have overcharged.
We find that this year, the fiscal year 1937, the interest on the governmental debt of Saskatchewan will be $7,039,000, constituting the largest single item in the whole of the expenditures of that province. What can they spend on education? They can spend $2,876,000 -and yet they must spend $7,039,000 for interest. They can spend $5,169,000 on public welfare, but they must spend $7,039,000 for interest. To-day debt charges amount to 49 per cent of ordinary expenditures and 52 per cent of ordinary revenue. It is the considered opinion of the provincial government that they cannot service that debt, unless they get further help from the dominion.
I suggest that in view of the great increase in private, municipal, provincial and dominion debts, when suggestions are made for some improvements or some change in public financing they should be given consideration, and should not be dismissed as though the last word had been spoken in regard to carrying on matters of public finance. It may be that the last word has not yet been said on the subject. It may be that it is possible to improve on our present system. In the past we have had cases where people, in their day and age, took the attitude, "We are the people, and wisdom will die with us." They took the stand that there could be no improvement in what they had conceived, or what had been conceived prior to their day and age. I submit that in connection with this question, likewise it is possible to have improvement in our way of handling public finance. I suggest that if failure to solve the question of public finance is weighing the people down so that they cannot attend to education, so that they cannot attend to public welfare, then it is high time that we looked into the matter very seriously.
What is the situation with regard to education? Let us consider for example, the university of Saskatchewan. I have been told by more than one professor of that university that he has received offers to go elsewhere, on much better pay, but that he hated to leave Saskatchewan in her hour of need. If there is one thing more than another that we need in Saskatchewan, it is the best scientists Canada can produce to study the means to

cope with drought, grasshoppers, smut, and all other pests and drawbacks the western farmer has to meet. The best scientists should be in the university of Saskatchewan, but we have not the money to pay them and keep them. Their salaries have been continually reduced, and we are asking them to work for mere pittances.
What is the position with regard to children who wish to have secondary education? The government in the province has done the best it can. It has used the radio; it has set up correspondence courses and has tried to cope with the situation. The fact remains however, that most of the children in the province -would like to have secondary education, but have not the money to spend in boarding in town or to pay the cost of reaching town.
Coming to the public schools we find that while in 1931 public school teachers received in salaries 86,695,000, in 1936 they received only $3,973,000. Those of us who live in Saskatchewan know of teacher after teacher who is working for no more than $300 a year. We know lots of them, young girls and young men, the finest Canadians one could find anywhere, who are teaching for less than enough to pay for board and lodgings and buy clothes for themselves, let alone books or magazines which would permit them to keep abreast of developments in education in other parts of the world. That is the way we are treating those people who are in charge of training the youth in Saskatchewan.
I suggest that it is highly dangerous to tell those teachers that all we can pay them for looking after our young people in Saskatchewan is sometimes as low as $300 a year. They hear, for example, that the dominion collects over $100,000,000 in income tax on a rate which is not high. They know, therefore, that there must be people in Canada who are receiving large sums of money from industry. They have heard about the textile inquiry; that five people each put $200,000 into a project and that those people got their money back, and in addition that during the thirty-one years that the project has been in existence they have each received an average annual income therefrom of over $97,000. They have been drawing that money right along, because they invested in a highly protected industry which used its tariff protection to overcharge the people. Some of them were prominent bankers. Perhaps they loaned credit to one another and invested no money of their own. The fact remains that they got their money back in about four years, and they have been drawing tuat average annual income ever since.

Put yourself, Mr. Speaker, in the place of a young woman out west whose duty it is to teach the children that this system of ours is fair and just; that the democratic system is better perhaps than the system they have in Russia or Germany; that it is fair; that it is the system the children should uphold and admire-a teacher who has an abiding conviction of the injustice and unfairness of the present system which practically condemns her to work for nothing, while other people, as she knows, on account of special privileges such as tariff policies are drawing money they have not earned in thousands and thousands of dollars. I ask, how can you expect her to have an influence favourable to our system on the children in her charge? When you mistreat in that way people who are in charge of the youth of the country, you can well expect that the young generation, when they grow to adulthood, will not have an abiding conviction in the fairness of democracy, and things may happen that we would shudder to see if we could only see them from this distance. The sooner we deal with that important problem the better for democracy in Canada. There is $900,000 in arrears of salary owing to these teachers, poorly paid as they are. Why? Because we have not the means of paying them. The government of Saskatchewan have struggled with that problem and the whole problem of carrying on our government under present conditions like veritable heroes as no one from another part of the dominion can ever appreciate, but they have not the financial means of dealing with it, and we in this house should take that into account.
I should like to deal shortly with the question of unemployment. There are many other things I should like to deal with, but I do not want to presume too long on the time of the house. In the information service for November, 1937, that was sent out by the national employment commission-this has been sent out, I suppose, to everybody, and so I am not guilty of any breach of confidence in reading it-I was surprised to find this statement:
In dealing with the problem of unemployment certain preliminary but essential steps have been taken.
Preliminary steps!
Relief has been "unscrambled" and clarified. Registration is revealing accurately the extent and nature of the problem.
This was in November, 1937. It goes on:
The migraney problem has been analysed and remedies suggested.
Thus the -way has been cleared for an attack on unemployment itself. The real problem of obtaining jobs for the employable unemployed, of which those on aid numbered 143,745, according to August registration returns, emerges. How is it to be met?

The Address-Mr. Tucker
Now how is it to be met? Two years after our party finds itself in office, after declaring that unemployment is Canada's greatest national problem, we are apparently still asking ourselves, how is that problem to be met? This is what I suggest, and I make the suggestion not with any desire to criticize the government but simply to help as a member of the Canadian House of Commons. The policy of the government with regard to trade is gradually solving the problem of unemployment; but if after two years in office we find that there are 143,000 employables still out of work and on aid, then I suggest that we should do something, while long range policies are absorbing them into industry, to look after these young fellows, to give them a chance to make a contribution to our national development in the meantime.
I was amazed, "floored," as a colleague of mine said, in the words of Mr. Micawber, when the last speaker was making some remark, when I read in the interim report of the national employment commission, at page 14, these words:
With the rapid improvement taking place in employment conditions in private industry, the commission decided to recommend that, at this stage of the recovery, not only should there be no expansion in public works programs, but that there should be a very substantial contraction in the total governmental expenditures for public works projects.
The hon. member has exhausted his right to speak.
Let him finish.
With the unanimous consent of the house.
But it is a part of it.

Yes, it is a part of it, but to-day not only is Germany rearming on a scale unprecedented in the history of any European nation but she is embarking at the same time on a program of building roads and public buildings, and land reclamation, for farming purposes, on a scale that Germany has never seen before. If Germany, hemmed in by the problems which face her, and rearming on a scale the like of which probably no European nation formerly ever saw, can find the means for a really comprehensive building program, can construct buildings which will stand as monuments for all time to the Hitler regime, can proceed with a vast program of public roads, can carry on important land reclamation schemes-if she can do these things after going through a tremendous war and all that it entailed, why is it that we in the Dominion of Canada cannot handle our small unemployment problem? Why is it that we are content to tell these young people, year after year, " We are registering you, and our long range policies will ultimately take care of you?" We believe they will; I believe they will; but I say in the meantime, supposing it requires another two or three years to develop those policies, should we not give them a chance to do something for the development of their country in the meantime?
The Address-Mr. Tucker

The mover and seconder of the address acquitted themselves, I think, very well upon their first attempt in this honourable chamber. Of course they endeavoured to give credit to the government for any improvement in Canada and particularly for any increases in trade. Supporters of the government are prone to do this kind of thing, and in doing so, to make comparisons between the years 1935 and 1937. In my opinion any credit for increases in trade and improvement in our general condition is due to the former government, and particularly to the United Kingdom agreement which was passed under that government, and if hon. members would go back and examine what happened in 1933-34 and 1934-35 they would find that a normal increase started at that time and that what we have had in the last year or so is only what might have been expected. I believe, however, that if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) would compare, as regards our trade with the United States, what happened in November, 1936, with what occurred in November, 1937, he would find something to give him cause for a little alarm.
We have listened during the last few days, and particularly to-day and yesterday, to some very interesting speeches. With reference to the speeches made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross), the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutoh) and the one to which we have just listened by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), as well as the references that have been made to the brief presented by the province of Saskatchewan to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, I do not believe that any greater evidence could be produced than is to be found in these speeches, of the failure of the Liberal party, both in the dominion and in Saskatchewan, since 1921.
I say that for this reason. From 1921 to 1930 the Liberals were in power in the federal arena, and since Saskatchewan entered confederation as a province the Liberals have been in control there except from 1929 to 1934, the most critical period in that province. In the federal field the Conservative party was in power from 1930 to 1935, another very critical period so far as the dominion is concerned. Apart from these two periods the Liberal party has been in control. Why then has it not done the things which these gentlemen tell us should have been done? They had an opportunity to do them. The hon. member for Moose Jaw, in particular, if he is so widely at variance with his party, might have moved an amendment or perhaps might have formed a new western party to bring about the results he would like to see attained. But he admitted that he had not accomplished very much here.
There are two or three paragraphs in the speech from the throne to which I should like to refer. The first is with reference to the proposed amendment of the constitution to provide for unemployment insurance. Had the government been as anxious, when they were in opposition, to see an unemployment insurance measure enacted and put upon the statute books as apparently they are to-day, when they would like to see all parties in the house in support of such a measure, we would have had an unemployment insurance scheme in operation to-day.
The next point to which I would refer is the reorganization of the Department of Agriculture. As we all know, agriculture is our most important industry. Production, processing and grading, and the marketing of our primary products-these are the all important things. The Department of Agriculture needed reorganization, and to prove that, I could go back to 1930 and quote the words of the then Minister of Agriculture, the hon. member for Melville. At that time he said that a new foundation would have to be laid for agriculture if we were to save the towns and villages of the west. I believe that some progress was made, certainly in the way of improving some of our products-cattle, bacon and certain other products that I could enumerate. Obstacles were removed and there was vast improvement during the period from 1930 to 1935. In that statement he tries to place the responsibility for what happened with respect to certain riots which took place in Regina, and that responsibility he lays at the door of the federal government of that day. That is a wrong impression, for if any government is to be charged with that responsibility it is the government which was in power in Saskatchewan at that time-and the present Minister of Agriculture happened to be the head of that government as premier. His government at that time encouraged the rioters, the trekkers, to proceed to Ottawa, and when the order was issued prohibiting them from going further he took strong exception to it. In proof of that I would refer to the report of the commission that was set up to investigate the Regina riots. The report was released on June 16, 1936, by the Hon. Mr. Estey, acting for the attorney general. The finding of the royal commission is given, and the personnel of the commission is set out. I need not go over that. The commission's finding was to this effect. They declared the leadership of the trek to be definitely communistic. The commissioners found that the federal government was quite justified in halting the march at Regina, because it would have menaced the peace, order and good government of every town or city in which they stopped.
